subtopic: BRETTON WOODS AND RELATED AGREEMENTS ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I compliment the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) for probably one of the shortest ministerial speeches
on record. I beg the indulgence of the House if I do not quite follow his standard because I believe third reading of this Bill is an opportunity to comment and deal with issues arising out of the Act and the present state of the international financial system. I believe this House should spend a few minutes in contemplation and examination of where we stand as a country and where the system itself stands.
As some Members of the House will know, both I and the Hon. Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly) returned yesterday from a quite extensive trip to Central America, Nicaragua in particular. We had an opportunity to view first hand a Third World country struggling with enormous economic problems, to say nothing of the war which is viciously exacerbating those problems. We saw the importance of the international economic system to a small country like that and how poorly the system is working for those countries at this time.
We had an opportunity to speak with the Minister of Economic Development who said that coffee, the major export commodity of that country, had suffered a price decline in the last several months. As a result, that country will be facing an additional shortfall of some $250 million in its current accounts. Such a drop in national income goes beyond the abstract statistics for a country of three million people with a GNP of $3 billion. It means that people there can no longer have the foreign exchange to buy replacement machinery parts for their tractors. It means that consumer goods such as toothpaste and shampoo which must be imported can no longer be afforded except with the use of American dollars.
In other words, the shortfalls in the system create the kinds of pressures in a country like that which not only result in major inconvenience in the daily lives of its people, but also eviscerate the economic capacity of that country.
It is not that there is a lack of effort, because the will and the expectation to rebuild the economy is foremost in everyone's mind. One cannot be anything but full of admiration for a poor country that is making every possible effort for land reform, to transfer land into the hands of the peasants of that country so they can, for the first time, have the responsibility to be independent and responsible for their self-sufficiency. But how can they do so when they do not have tractors or irrigation pumps?
First, there is an embargo by the U.S., which we implicitly accept, and second, the international economic system no longer affords them the ability to sell their commodities at a

September 18, 1987
Bretton Woods and Related Agreements Act
fair rate in order to achieve the kind of economic revenue that is required to maintain a minimum of growth.
When considering this Bill, the purpose of which is to set up a new credit system, we must ask whether we are lecturing on navigation while the ship is going down. Are we tinkering with minor repairs to the system when the system itself has some very basic flaws?
It is time for a new Bretton Woods Agreement. It is time to rethink the agreement, rather than simply tinker around the margins of the system.
When the major countries of the world came together at Bretton Woods to sign a new economic agreement on trade and international finance in 1944, conditions were very different from what they are now. The United States not only had a generosity of spirit and a belief and commitment to multilateralism, the American dollar stood as the primary and unassailable world currency. Both those conditions have changed. Certainly, the attitude of the present U.S. administration does not reflect that same commitment to multilateralism and generosity of spirit. Rather, we see an attempt to play Rambo-like politics on the economic frontiers.
In addition, the United States no longer has the economic dominance it had 30 or 40 years ago. One need only look at their own situation. They have gone from being the largest creditor nation in the world to the largest debtor nation in the world, running the largest trade deficit of any country. The only way the United States is able to support that huge deficit is by borrowing from abroad, primarily from the Japanese who now hold some $55 billion of equity and holdings in the United States economy alone.
The obvious result is that there is no longer a world currency that can stabilize and facilitate the operation of the international economy. The dollar is subject to pressures and instabilities, as evidenced by the insecurity on the world stock markets. We are seeing a curious situation in which we are trying to evade the issue of incredible problems in Third World countries. We have been trying to manage these situations on a case-by-case basis, yet knowing that every major international bank, including Canadian banks, have outstanding debts. If a bank decided to pull a card from the deck representing these outstanding debts, the whole deck would fall.
Recently, major Canadian banks had to set aside hundreds of millions of dollars, which only represent approximately one-quarter of those outstanding debts. The debt problem is being managed in a way that is designed almost to put a Draconian discipline on the debtor nations, and to serve the banking interests more than to encourage economic growth in these countries.
These countries are in a Catch 22 situation. They cannot stimulate growth in their economies because of the restrictive measures imposed upon them. All their export earnings must go to servicing the debt, so there is nothing left to reinvest into those countries to stimulate further development.
At the same time, economic aid is being pulled back by the wealthy nations in the world and commodity prices are falling. One would have to refer to the Book of Job for a text on the international economic system, where it states: "My God, why hast thou forsaken me?"
This deluge of incredible problems requires a reorganization of the system by the major players in the world. They must recognize that the U.S. currency is no longer the foundation of the international system and certainly cannot be in the future. There must be a different arrangement on our exchange rates. We must find a better solution to the debt problem than the case-by-case approach which has been adopted thus far. We must find a way of dealing with the commodity problems in the world economy, recognizing that the so-called market system we have adopted has only resulted in driving prices down and creating more instability, of which we are partly victim, and from which there is no result. The longer we simply try to tinker with the system, the worse the problem will get.
This brings me to the matter of political management. I believe the problems of the world economy have far superseded the capacity to manage them. Once again, it is a case where economics is far ahead of politics. We have not yet combined our ideas and resources to find ways to manage the system. In fact, looking at recent events, we would have to conclude that we are going in reverse. We may be running the risk of falling back even further, with ruptures in the system and a retreat back into the era of the 1930s where we had country pitted against country and regional block against regional block.
I suppose what I regret most is that that is a reflection also of what seems to be happening in our own country. Clearly, the case we tried to make over the past two and one-half years is that the present Government of Canada has fallen into a basic fallacy, that is, that our economic interests could be best served through bilateral relationships. Most obvious, was the attempt to negotiate a free trade deal with the United States. Instead of using our efforts, energies and imagination to try to provide leadership in the international economic system, we were also part of that retreat into protectionism, into the North America fortress. We were pulling our commitments back and that was a tragedy because at the original Bretton Woods Agreement, our own country was one of the major advocates of a new international economic order. We were one of the architects of that system. We provided much of the intelligence and recommendations which helped build Bretton Woods at the outset.
It has been of great regret to my Party, and we have said this right from the beginning that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) announced that the economic priority of Canada was a free trade deal with the United States. We asked if this meant we were abandoning our multilateral commitment? Are we retreating from the international priority we once had? The answer, of course, is yes. The people who have won out in the
September 18, 1987

decision-making councils of Ottawa have been the bilateralists, the Simon Reismans and the Derek Burneys, the Brian Mulroneys and the others-and I use the name in a generic sense, Mr. Speaker, in referring to the Prime Minister-the North Americans, the continentalists who have dominated our economic thinking; not the internationalists not the multilater-alists, not those who saw in this country the opportunity and responsibility to try to reforge, remake, redefine and help reform the international economic system.
We have made a fundamental mistake. We have taken the wrong course and we have applied our energies in the wrong direction. As a result, we are now paying the price. We do not know what kind of strange combination arrangement will emerge on October 5, but we know now that the promises and expectations that were raised for that North American trade deal have been shot through with holes. It is not going to be the great economic cornucopia, and resolution to all the problems. It will not have a dispute settling mechanism. It is not going to provide for that open access. It is not going to provide for all those promises that were made. The fact is that we have allowed three years to go by and have won nothing as a result.
In the meantime, we have had to face a growing cloud and shadow in the international economic environment. We have abandoned many of our allies and friends. We have pulled back on our economic interests. One example is the trade performance of Canada last year. In every single region of the world, with the exception of the United States, our trade fell drastically, sometimes as much as 30 per cent and 40 per cent. At the same time, the Department of External Affairs was cutting back 30 per cent on our Export Development Fund, closing embassies, and consulates, and cutting back on export promotion everywhere except the United States of America. As a result, the dependency we have on that one country for our own trade was even more severe and extreme.
We have been abandoning our international commitments. We have gone asleep at the switch in terms of opening up new trade opportunities. The fastest growing economic region of the world has been in the Pacific Rim. The OECD country which has the lowest rate of trade in the Pacific Rim is our own country. We are making very little effort to try to recapture that area. The drops are severe.
At the same time, we have been facing, along with many Third World countries, major declines in the prices for our commodities. In certain respects we have a lot more in common with Malaysia, Latin America and Asia than we do with the United States, because our major exports are still earned through our commodities sales-our grain, forest products and minerals. Those are the commodities which have been suffering the ravages of an international economic system which is out of order.
Instead of applying ourselves and trying to come to grips with the need to get new commodity agreements, to provide stability of prices, to secure access to markets internationally,
Brelton Woods and Related Agreements Act
we have been spending all our time negotiating with the United States. Our eye has been on the wrong spiral. We have substantially missed the target. As a result, I think the world has lost a country which has in the past provided economic leadership in these matters, one which has reached out to establish a commitment and understanding and belief in international economic order.
Perhaps the primary missing ingredient is that voice in international councils trying to bring together a new meaning to a Bretton Woods type agreement. Obviously, it would be more complicated and more difficult than it was in 1944. Obviously, it is one that would have to include a much broader range of participants, with a much broader and more varied range of economic interests.
The world is not the oyster of the western hemisphere. We in the western hemisphere and Europe can no longer set the pace and dominate the world as we once could. There are many more increasingly influential economic players in the economic game, so of course the rules will have to be changed. The rules will not always be our own way. It is time we faced up to that reality. It is time we stopped hiding from that reality and began to apply ourselves in an effort to reorganize and reform the international system to meet that reality.
The Bill before us is acceptable. No one is arguing with it. There is some modest repair of the system. But it does not tackle the fact that presently there is an obvious and clear discrimination in the international banking system towards Third World countries, particularly if they are politically unacceptable to the United States. If the United States does not like the policies of a Third World country, it is not going to get loans from the International Development Bank. That is very clear. We cannot tolerate that. That is not the way an international rule of law should operate. It should not have ideological overtones. That is not the new international economic reality we must face. But we say nothing about that.
We know that the incredible weakness of the commodity markets is forcing many of those Third World countries into positions of utter desperation. Again, the voice of Canada has been stilled on that matter. We are not arguing, as we should be, in world council for effective commodity agreements. We buy once again a position from our ideological friend to the south, and everything has to be the open-market system. It is not working for us and it is not working for them. It is time we began to look at the need for forms of agreements which would provide that stability.
The international banking system is no longer dealing effectively with the debt problems of the Third World. We are simply putting off the accounting to a future date, perhaps for another generation. It is interesting when we talk about domestic orders, from time to time to hear Conservative Members of Parliament saying we have to control the debt here domestically because we do not want future generations to pay the bill.

September 18, 1987
Bretton Woods and Related Agreements Act
Should we not raise the same question internationally? Should we not be asking the same type of questions with respect to how we propose to do that in the world market which, in many ways, has far more impact on us? Should we not also be asking what currency will make the world go round? What will be the medium of exchange if the U.S. dollar falls and falters as it has been for the last few years? It has been devalued by almost 20 per cent against the Japanese yen.
I suppose my regret is that those were not the kinds of issues or questions I heard or saw addressed by the Minister of State for Finance or by the Government in bringing this Bill before us.
1 pay my compliments to the Chairman of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade who is in the Chamber. Elis committee will study this issue in the fall. It is an important issue. I pay my compliments to the Chairman for giving leadership in this area. However, we now have a Bill before us on this matter. It is here in the House today at third reading stage. I thought that the opportunity to raise these matters would have been before us. As I say, I know the reason why it was not. 1 know the preoccupation and obsession that has so dominated the thinking of the Government in terms of the North American economic trade system. Its relationships only with the United States has pushed out consideration of all other matters. It has blinded us to the wider perspectives of those international responsibilities.
I hope that as we approach the denouement of that particular preoccupation and members of the Conservative caucus realize just what a tortured road they have been following and what kind of false expectations and hopes they have been creating we can get back to reality and get back to what I believe is the Canadian stewardship and task; that is to say, to provide leadership on the multilateral international economic front where we can do some good, where we can try to reorganize the rules as well as try to reformulate the Bretton Woods Agreements in trade and finance. We can try to use the capacity of our leadership to mobilize other countries to bring about that type of commitment to reform. I believe that is an honourable, useful and important calling for Canada. It is one that I hope we will soon adopt.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to make a few remarks on third reading of Bill C-68, which introduces changes to the Bretton Woods and Related Agreements Act which will give Canada authority to participate in the Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency, or MIGA as it is known.
MIGA will be able to provide insurance for foreign investors in Third World countries against non-commercial risks. The annual report of the World Bank for 1986 states that there are four categories of non-commercial risk which will be covered in particular. They are: the transfer risk resulting from host
government restrictions on conversion and transfer; the risk of loss resulting from legislative or administrative action or omission of the host government which has the effect of depriving the investor of ownership, control, or substantial benefit from his investment; the risk resulting from the repudiation of a contract by the host government when the investor has no access to a competent forum, faces unreasonable delays in such a forum, or is unable to enforce a final judgment; and, finally, the risk of war and civil disturbances.
The establishment of MIGA is in general accord with the recommendations of the Brandt Commission on north-south relations. Certainly, there are advantages to seeing this type of an insurance scheme that we hope will promote increased investment in the Third World. That kind of investment flow is very important. On the face of it there are advantages both to developing and developed countries in this type of process. There are advantages to Canadian business in establishing MIGA.
MIGA has particular advantages in view of the problems that have developed in terms of loans to Third World countries over the last few years. These loans have crippled the economies of Third World countries. We have the debt crisis where countries such as Mexico, Brazil and Peru face astronomical debt servicing charges that no one expects they will be able to meet in any reasonable way. The countries of Africa, which have been crippled by famine and drought, have also been crippled by the debt loads that they have upon them. At the same time this debt structure threatens the stability of the financial system in the developed world because if some of these debtors default, that can cause a major problem with the banking systems of North America and Europe.
There are a great many advantages, on the face of it, to a system that instead of providing loans to Third World countries looks to equity investment. This means that developing countries would see only an out-flow of dollars when a venture had become profitable instead of payments having to be made whether the venture is profitable or not, as with a loan. From the point of view of the developed countries that we hope will be doing the investing, the investors would realize that a profit was required. They would invest only after they had looked twice. There would be a more realistic assessment of the risk, something that did not happen in the heady days of making some of the loans that took place in the late 1970s.
Equity investment can also create major long-term problems for the countries that receive the immediate stimulus of the investment. There can be the loss of control over key economic sectors, which is something that the present Conservative Government does not seem to recognize, or does not care about, when it comes to Canada's own economy. However, it is something that is of concern to several Third World countries. They find themselves between a rock and hard place. They know that on the one hand they need the in-flow of capital, while on the other they are very concerned that equity investment can result in a permanent loss of any control over their own economies.
September 18, 1987

This is the crux of the whole international economic situation. Are countries in the Third World going to have some control over their own economies or will those economies be managed out of New York, London, Tokyo and West Germany?
The major situation that we need to face in terms of the developing countries is that while there are increasing costs for inputs they face declining commodity prices. I would just like to quote from the World Bank annual report which discusses non-oil commodity prices:
The dollar price of nonoil commodity exports from the developing countries declined by about 10 percent in 1985.
A decline of 10 per cent in commodity prices for countries that are already poor means that these countries have to cut back their standard of living by at least 10 per cent and more when we consider that the inputs they require in terms of oil and machinery have all gone up in price. The report goes on:
This drop was caused both by slow demand growth since early 1985 in industrial countries and, in the case of grains, cotton, and oilseeds, by excess supply resulting from exceptionally bountiful crops or shifts in the price-support and export policies of major suppliers.
When prices drop for Third World countries they often respond by producing more. Our whole economic system is based on the fact that in order to compete people have to produce more. When everybody produces more it creates a glut in the market and, as a result, commodity prices fall further.
The report also stated:
Producing countries, in need of export earnings to finance imports and debt service, have given few signs of restraining production in the face of falling prices. The average dollar price of metals and minerals fell by 5 per cent and has declined by about 30 per cent since 1980.
Tin prices fell dramatically, and trading in tin was suspended at the London Metal Exchange in late October when the International Tin Council ran into financial difficulties and could no longer support the price of tin.
Food prices in dollar terms declined by an average of 12 per cent, after a 6 per cent increase in 1984. The price of beverages, however, picked up substantially during the fourth quarter of 1985, influenced strongly by the coffee boom, the result of a severe drought that is expected to reduce Brazil's 1986/87 coffee crop by between 30 per cent and 50 per cent.
Bad news in Brazil where there was a drought meant good news for coffee producers in other parts of the world. That was the only possibility of good news. Since then the price of coffee has gone down. The report further states:
The price of tea, however, declined to about half its 1984 level by the end of 1985, following large increases in production in tea producing countries. The prices of cereals and fats and oils dropped by 66 per cent and 24 per cent, respectively.
Imagine a drop of 24 per cent in the price of basic commodity exports. The report further states:
World cotton acreage increased by 11 per cent in 1984/85 in response to favourable prices the year before; world prices for cotton then fell 21 per cent in the 1984/85 season. Since then, however, the United States and China, both major cotton producers, have taken measures to reduce cotton production.
Bretton Woods and Related Agreements Act
That report is from The World Bank, a conservative organization that is not given to making extravagant claims.
The drop in commodity prices and the effect on Third World countries is the primary problem that we face. While we pat ourselves on the back for passing this law which will make it easier for investors to move into Third World countries, we must ask if it would have made any difference if the inflow of funds in the late 1970s to Third World countries had been in the form of equity investment, as this law provides for and gives some assurance for, or if it had been in the form of loans, as happened.
When commodity prices drop and input prices increase, it does not matter what the situation is. The economies of those countries are in serious difficulty. Sooner or later we will have to confront that situation. We cannot have it both ways. We cannot have an international trading structure that robs developing countries of a fair price for their commodities, and at the same time hope to have a stable investment and loan climate in those same countries.
I wish to turn to the analogy of the prairie farm in the late 1930s. My father lost a farm in Saskatchewan at that time. I do not think it would have mattered a great deal if he had had someone else who had invested and taken a share of the farm profits, rather than having a mortgage that he was unable to pay because of poor crops and prices. It would have meant that he was a sharecropper instead of a bankrupt farmer. I do not think there is a great deal of difference in the economic status of those two.
The Bretton Woods agreements were reached at the end of the Second World War in order to attempt to stabilize the international economic situation. It would be interesting to look at some of the expectations that we had at that time.
In July, 1943, Henry Morgenthau, the then Secretary of the Treasury in the United States, produced a preliminary draft outline of a proposal for an international stabilization fund of the United Associated Nations. At that time he stated that "monetary stabilization, commercial policy, the provision of long-term international credit, promotion of stability in the prices of primary products, and arrangements for relief and rehabilitation are problems that join at innumerable points", and that they had to be dealt with separately and then integrated.
He also stated that there were, "three inseparable monetary tasks: to prevent the disruption of foreign exchanges, to avoid the collapse of monetary systems, and to facilitate the restoration and balanced growth of international trade", which all required international action.
He pointed to the need to avoid the "repetition of exchange instability and monetary collapse that followed the last war", that is, the 1914-1918 war. He called for an international stabilization fund. He pointed out that while some people wished to have one agency look after all the different concerns, the United States wished to have separate agencies. He also

September 18, 1987
Bretton Woods and Related Agreements Act
stated that for the fund to work needs co-operation "to reduce trade barriers and to terminate discriminatory practices that have in the past hampered the balanced growth of international trade. The nations of the world can be prosperous only if they are good neighbours in their economic as well as their political relations".
He also stated, "world prosperity like world peace is indivisible". We need to learn that lesson, yet we have a system where we are attempting to defend and develop a fortress-like mentality that allows some people in some nations of the world to exist in a degree of prosperity, and even in our own nation, there are huge gaps of poor people, while other nations live in total and absolute poverty with very little hope of getting out of the morass of debt and underdevelopment. As long as we have a system that perpetuates unjust commodity prices compared with high input costs, this situation will continue.
Like the previous speaker, I had a chance to visit Nicaragua last week with the Canadian Mission for Peace. One of the things that impressed me most, apart from the spirit of the people and their commitment to the revolution and the hope for peace, was the inflation. We had to carry a small bag of money in order to purchase lunch or supper.
That country is suffering from a United States embargo designed to cripple its economy, it is suffering a surrogate war with the United States paying the mercenary Contras to fight against and destroy development.
We visited a small co-operative in the hills of Nicaragua far from anywhere where a group of some 11 families were attempting to develop self-sufficiency and an economy where they could look after themselves. This was not a strategic economic unit in Nicaragua, except from the point of view that it was enabling those people to feed themselves. This place, where 11 families were living, was the target of a Contra attack, financed by the United States. The Contras came down in the middle of the night, attacked these people, destroyed their homes, burnt their tractors, and forced them to flee. Then those families returned and tried to rebuild.
This is the reality of what is happening in Nicaragua where the Government is trying to work with its people to develop a decent economy and where the United States is doing everything it can to destabilize that economy. The result is the kind of inflation about which I was speaking, inflation which is making it very difficult for that country to survive and for ordinary people to survive.
This is very germane to the topic which we are discussing. We hope that there will be increased investment in Third World countries, and we hope that it will result in improvements in the living standards of those countries. I emphasize that we must address the fundamental problems of peace and the fundamental problems of an unjust economic structure. Unless we are prepared to do that, the proposals for increased
investment and for providing insurance for that investment will not amount to very much.
While we support the proposal, we urge the Government to make its voice heard on the international scene and to speak out in favour of peace for countries like Nicaragua, which means no more funding for the Contras who are waging war on the people of Nicaragua. Also our country must speak out for a just economic policy which will provide fair commodity prices.
As well our country must realize the commitment made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) during the last election, the commitment which was made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) when he spoke before the United Nations in 1984, that is, to move toward .7 per cent of our Gross National Product being provided for official development assistance. That commitment was made in good faith before the United Nations, but they have done nothing but welsh and back away from it. Other nations are doing the same thing, but that does not make it any better for Canada to be doing it.
Developing nations need an infusion of development assistance to develop their own economies. I urge the Government not to pat itself on the back for providing this insurance system for private investment in Third World countries. 1 think that is important, but even more important is tackling the question of commodity prices and reducing the threat of war and military expenditures in Third World countries.

Madam Speaker, I was very glad to hear both previous speakers on this subject, but 1 would like to ask the Hon. Member for Cowichan-Malahat-The Islands (Mr. Manly) to explain further his concern about trading debt for equity, having Canadian, American, or other lending countries buy up local industries or utilities with the debt that the country owes us where those industries and utilities exist. I assume the reason it would be worth while acquiring that equity is that the owners of the money in our country would expect to make money; they do not expect to lose money.
Does the Hon. Member envisage that when those countries give up the equity in their factories, their railways, or whatever it may be in exchange for their foreign debt, it will mean that they have less income in the country, lower wages perhaps, and less dividend? Second, will it have any effect in reducing inflation? Third, will there still be more debt? Will it stop the debt process, or will the debt arise again? Finally, what will happen when there is no more equity to sell off?

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his question. I think this is an extremely important situation.
Given the very high debts of a number of countries, there is a process by which other people are purchasing those in exchange for equity. What we need to realize is that Third World countries are not poor countries when it comes to resources. Third World countries are often extremely rich in
September 18, 1987

resources. What they do not have is control over the development of their own resources and control over the prices for which those resources are being sold on the international market.
When some of the oil producing countries got control back in the 1970s and OPEC became a very powerful cartel, we saw how the price of oil immediately went up very significantly, which resulted in some very severe shocks to all parts of the world.
If developing countries had more control over their own resources, we would be in a completely different situation. However, when people purchase equity, they are really purchasing control over resources. We have seen it in Canada in the past where our resources ended up being in the hands of foreign multinationals. This means that we as a nation have not had the capacity or ability to mould our own economic future in the way we would have liked.
I think the purchase of loans for equity will result in less control and will result in a continuing outflow of money from Third World countries, because the people who are making the purchases are still looking to get a good return. There will be a continuing outflow of money and, in addition, there will be a loss of control.

Mr. Speaker, 22 per cent of homeless Canadians are women-older women, single mothers, sick women. Before a national conference on accommodation for the homeless, National Action Committee on the Status of Women President Louise Dulude and Mrs. Claudette Godley, co-ordinator of Montreal's "Chez Doris" home for women, both stated that poverty is the main reason why women are homeless or living in substandard housing. The Minister responsible for the Status of Women (Mrs. McDougall) issued a press release full of pious wishes in which she concludes by expressing hope that the conference will go a long way towards improving housing conditions for women.
Mr. Speaker, knowing as we do that the Minister responsible for housing did not announce anything new at the conference, that the Minister responsible for the Status of Women paid lip service to the cause, and that this Government did not even bother to address the 600 demonstrators of the Front d'action populaire en reamenagement urbain who marched on Parliament Hill last Tuesday, we can only conclude that this Government simply does not have the political will to solve the homeless problem.

subtopic: CONDOLENCES TO FAMILIES OF THREE VICTIMS OF NORITA MINE ACCIDENT AT MATAGAMI
CONDOLENCES TO FAMILIES OF THREE VICTIMS OF NORITA MINE ACCIDENT AT MATAGAMI
speechtext:
Yesterday, Mr. Speaker, the people of Abitibi were shocked when they heard about the fatal accident which took the lives of three men working 2,000 feet underground on a drilling platform at Matagami's Norita Mine, a subsidiary of Noranda.
The victims are Marco Turcotte, a 22-year old married man, and two single men, Gilles Laplante and Henri Widz, aged 32 and 30 respectively. All three were Val-d'Or residents working for R.M. Limited, a drilling firm.
One third of the work had been completed when the accident occurred. The team had finished its shift and the platform was halfway up level 11-50 feet from ground level-when one of the walls of the hole collapsed above them, dragging them down their fatal fall.
The drilling company has been operating in Val-d'Or for six years and this is the first such accident.

September 18, 1987
5. Q. 21
As a former miner I can appreciate how these families feel and I offer them my condolences in their great hardshsip.

Mr. Speaker, in a Globe and Mail ad of September 17, Mr. Abbott, former director of the Canadian Immigration Service, downgrades those Canadians who are not Anglophones or Francophones of the professional class. Even though his poll contained many questions biased against immigrants, the multiculturalism answer nevertheless showed a clear majority of Canadians who want Canada to be made up of a diversity of people. In spite of that, Mr. Abbott and his wealthy friends want to shut out those coming from what he dismisses as the Third World.
By implication they ignore and insult Canada's Amerindians and Inuit whose land we continue to steal, they ignore and insult Canadians from China who put Canada's railway through the Rockies, Canadians from Japan who made the West Coast bloom till our Government imprisoned and robbed them, Canadians from northern, central and eastern Europe who ploughed and populated our Prairies, Canadians from Italy, Portugal, Greece and the Middle East who built and service our post-war cities, and Canadians from the Caribbean, Latin America and Asia who now do so many of our lowest paid jobs.
I call on the Government to repudiate this destructive action by a former director of the Canadian Immigration Service.

Mr. Speaker, the new frontier of space is upon us all, and as we as a nation take a quantum leap into the future we must make sure that we land with our collective feet on terra firma.
The proposed Canadian Space Agency will play the vital role in co-ordinating, managing and administering all of Canada's efforts in this exciting new challenge. The location of this agency is, therefore, vital.
Close, continuous co-operative efforts with many federal Departments, foreign countries, such as the U.S.A., Japan, the Soviet Union and members of the European Space Agency, are essential. Immediate access to the critical mass of scientists, scientific knowledge and many of Canada's leading research organizations, such as the National Research Council, the
Department of Communications and many high technology firms, is essential.
My colleagues, the Hon. Member for Ottawa West (Mr. Daubney), the Hon. Member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Tupper), and myself agree that the logical, rational, neutral and least expensive option for Canada's Space Agency is within our National Capital Region.

Mr. Speaker, recent studies show that one in five Canadians are illiterate. More than four million people cannot read or write well enough to function adequately in our society and one million more cannot read or write at all.
The problem of illiteracy spreads across all groups in society, regardless of age, economics or region. Some 60 per cent of the Canadian illiterate population are unemployed and are not looking for work. Most do not even qualify for government training programs because they have not accumulated enough years in school.
All Canadians can help solve the problem of illiteracy, but the federal Government has an especially critical role to play. The federal Government has the influence and resources necessary to begin a national war against illiteracy. The Government of Canada should begin by developing a national advertising campaign on illiteracy. Then the Government should follow it up with concrete, specific programs to assist those countless thousands of Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, today we are celebrating the birthday of an organization, an organization dedicated to preserving peace and security for the people of the North American continent.
This year we observe the thirtieth anniversary of the inauguration of the North American Aerospace Defence Command. I am pleased that our Government's defence White Paper commits Canada to continuing our partnership in NORAD. Like any good partnership, NORAD is an experience in sharing, sharing the duties, sharing information, sharing the risks, and sharing the satisfaction of contributing to a strong and vigilant North America. NORAD is a successful, vibrant, binational commitment.
September 18, 1987

On this thirtieth anniversary I congratulate all those who have contributed to this success, to the future benefits to which we look forward, and to the way in which NORAD enhances our prospects for peace and security.

Mr. Speaker, this week Canadians have received four strong messages regarding hockey violence.
Yesterday the NHL, finally succumbing to public pressure, has moved to try to end bench-clearing brawls by instituting hefty fines and suspensions. Unfortunately, the NHL has not chosen to deal directly with individual fighting. Yesterday as well the federal Government's Commission on Fair Play unveiled its media campaign aimed at reducing violence in minor hockey through a series of shock-value ads that show it as repulsive. It is a good start, Mr. Speaker.
We also received bad news. In Estevan, Saskatchewan, this week a junior hockey player from North Dakota received a fractured vertebra during an exhibition game Wednesday night. There have been 107 spinal cord injuries in the past 13 years. Half of these hockey players have become paraplegics or quadriplegics.
Finally, Canada and the world saw that you can play hockey hard and Fight-free of violence and draw millions of viewers. The Canada Cup showed us that if hockey is good, fast, clean, and most of all competitive, we do not need the goons at any level to attract the crowds.
Let us continue the campaign to remove violence and injury from our ice rinks.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a good many newspaper articles recently drew our attention to the plight of homeless men and women who are denied access to temporary shelter. In a number of cases these are psychiatric patients who are not sick enough to be given a bed in an institution, but who are unable to live alone. In other cases they are individuals suffering from chronic alcoholism or drug abuse. In all cases, Mr. Speaker, they create a major problem: they are very likely to disturb other tranquility-seeking homeless people.
The Ottawa Citizen related the case of six women who were denied access to temporary shelter. Last week, 49-year-old Kenneth Ryan of Halifax, a vagrant well known to the police and suffering from particular problems, was killed.
This week, Mr. Speaker, in Montreal's Jeanne-Mance Park, a seriously injured older woman was found lying in a sleeping bag next to a suitcase containing all her personal belongings.
Can such destitute people be abandoned on the streets? I urge the Government to show leadership and provide community homes before winter for these homeless people who are suffering from problems which prevent them from using the same facilities as other homeless people.

subtopic: NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY-MINING-POSITION ON FLOWTHROUGH SHARES
NEW DEMOCRATIC PARTY-MINING-POSITION ON FLOWTHROUGH SHARES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the mining exploration depletion allowance is a critical component of the tax rules which make flow-through shares attractive to investors. On December 16 last, in considering Bill C-23, the NDP finance critic denounced the flow-through shares. He said:
I decided that where you have a measure which should fundamentally be
rethought, we should simply tell the Government to stop it, take the measure
away, start all over again and strike out the loophole.

September 18, 1987
Last night during finance hearings on tax reform and the specific proposal to phase out the mining exploration depletion allowance, the same NDP finance critic was heard to endorse flow-through shares, the same flow-through shares he asked the Government to strike out nine short months earlier.
Why this flip-flop? The NDP finance critic answered the question himself last night when he said that it had been brought to his attention that there are 25 or 30 ridings across northern Canada in which this is an important issue.
Let no one think members of the NDP are prepared to let principles stand in the way of political expediency. Just watch them change their policies as often as they change their clothes.

Mr. Speaker, following our visit to Nicaragua last week, the Mission for Peace is convinced that Canada can play a key role both in persuading the United States that a peaceful solution in that area is possible, and in reinforcing international momentum for peace.
Specifically, the mission recommends that Canada take a stronger, more clear position against any further funding of the Contras.
Second, it recommends that Canada should offer to participate directly in the verification process through multilateral channels, including the United Nations, and to provide financial resources to the process in addition to the offer of technical expertise.
Third, it recommends that Canada take the lead in forming a special emergency reconstruction fund as recommended by the Caracas, meeting and fourth, establish a diplomatic presence in Managua.
Fifth, it recommends that Canada increase bilateral aid to Nicaragua based on Nicaragua's proven ability to administer and effectively deliver aid and the urgent needs which exist in the country, and that Canada examine ways to improve export-import relationships in Central America.
Sixth, the committee recommended that Canada urge the United States to lift the trade embargo as a sign of good faith in the peace process, and examine ways of improving the means of transportation between Nicaragua and Canada.
Seventh, Canada should offer aid for transitional measures such as the reconciliation commissions and the resettlement and integration of those granted amnesty, and eighth, develop a comprehensive Central American policy. I urge the Government to follow these recommendations.

subtopic: PROGRESSIVE CONSERVATIVE PARTY'S PARLIAMENTARY NEWS SERVICE
PROGRESSIVE CONSERVATIVE PARTY'S PARLIAMENTARY NEWS SERVICE

That will probably save a lot of money considering he will not have to kick in his television set quite so often.

The true version: Minister forced to resign after wife obtains a $2 million interest-free loan. The TNN version: Minister takes sabbatical to study wife's creative financing skills.
True version: Prime Minister spends $350,000 of Tory funds to renovate house and build closet for Gucci shoes. TNN version: Prime Minister creates jobs, jobs, jobs for European shoe manufacturer.
The day after the next election the true version will be: Scandal-ridden Tory Government takes a beating at the polls. The TNN version will say: Inaccurate news coverage has led Canadians to believe that that there was a slight decrease in Tory popularity.
Claire Hoy's book will come out shortly as well. It will lambaste the Prime Minister for patronage and lifestyle-

In light of the fact that Firestone has not given an indication one way or the other, what action has the federal Government taken to ensure that Firestone is operating in good faith?
I have suggested on numerous occasions that rather than have the Minister for Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. de Cotret) send civil servants to Akron, Ohio, in order to get the message to Firestone that the company had better bargain in good faith and be prepared to do everything possible to save those 1,300 jobs, he should carry that message himself to
September 18, 1987

Akron, Ohio. It is not enough to leave 1,300 jobs up to civil servants. The Minister and the Government must show some leadership. I urge the Minister to book a flight to Akron this weekend to ensure that Firestone is bargaining in good faith in order to save those 1,300 Hamilton jobs.

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Prime Minister I will direct my question to the Deputy Prime Minister. Sulphuric gas pollution in the United States is affecting our health and our economy, our lakes, our rivers and our forests, and our buildings and agriculture. Last April President Reagan made a statement in this Chamber which led the Prime Minister to conclude that there had been a tremendous breakthrough for Canada on acid rain.
Given those facts, will the Deputy Prime Minister admit that the Prime Minister wrongly led Canadians to believe that progress had taken place by saying that an agreement with the United States was a realistic possibility? Does he admit that, in substance, the bottom line is that no progress has been made on acid rain with the United States as indicated by the publication today of this study and scientific report by NAPAP?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, those accusations are absolutely false, but what is perhaps even more disquieting is that when we are faced again with a major challenge on the acid rain question, a question which is vital to the future of Canada, the official spokesman for the Official Opposition, instead of trying to join with the Government of Canada in pressing the case for alleviation of the acid rain problem, chooses to try to make petty, partisan points out of an issue that is too important for petty politics.
My colleague, the Minister of the Environment, who is unavoidably out of the House today because of a long-standing engagement with the Liberal Premier of Prince Edward Island, issued a strong press release and statement this morning. We are challenging on a scientific basis the scientific evidence put forward by NAPAP. We understand it is not the position of the President of the United States. We intend to carry Canada's case and to protect Canada's interest. I would invite the co-operation of other Hon. Members of the House.

Mr. Speaker, I would join in supporting the Government if its policies on acid rain had been credible so far, but they have been just a sequence of public relation stunts and nothing more than that.
Oral Questions CANADIAN POSITION

Mr. Speaker, contrary to what the Secretary of State for External Affairs seems to believe, the NAPAP report is a report that was paid for by the U.S. administration, not by the scientific community of the U.S. Therefore, it is a political report.
I must ask the Secretary of State why he and the Prime Minister have been silent for the past week since John Campbell, an assistant administrator in the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, appeared before a U.S. congressional committee in opposition to an acid rain Bill that is being proposed there. What kind of attitude is that considering the promises made in this Chamber by President Reagan and the enthusiastic demonstrations of success the Prime Minister seemed to convey to the Canadian public? He made a big deal out of it.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the highly partisan spokesman for the Official Opposition and I are in agreement on one thing-the NAPAP report is a political report, not a scientific report. It pretends to be a scientific report. We are challenging its scientific basis.
I should make clear how that report came to be. It was not mandated by the administration, it was the result of an act of Congress. It is not yet the position of the U.S. administration. We trust it will not become so. However, if we are to ensure that Canada's interest in fighting acid rain is advanced, we have to continue the fight vigorously and not walk away from the table as the Hon. Member did when he was Minister of the Environment.

We always laugh at these desperate attempts of the Progressive Conservative Party to rewrite history. The Minister should know that the NAPAP report was written by 12 federal agencies, four national laboratories, and four presidential appointees. If that is not a statement by the administration I do not know what it is.

Mr. Speaker, I now have to raise with the Minister this sudden decision to spend money on a U.S. publicity campaign. In what is almost a deathbed repentance the Government decides in its fourth year to launch a publicity campaign on acid rain. Why did it not do it in its first year? As well, why not enlarge the budget to carry the campaign to New Brunswick and Nova Scotia where the Tory Governments have not yet signed the agreement?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I hope historians, when they read Hansard, will take a careful look at that question because it began by accusing the Government of doing nothing but public relations on acid rain throughout our first three years, and

September 18, 1987
Oral Questions
ended by asking why we did not mount a public relations campaign earlier in our mandate rather than now. The Elon. Member is answered by his own absurdity. However, 1 am not interested in exchanging partisan remarks with him.
Tie talks about rewriting history. Unhappily, he has no history to rewrite. What we are trying to do is protect not the history of Canada but the future of Canada against a very real threat from acid rain.
A report was brought down in the U.S. which purports to have a scientific basis. We believe it is scientifically incomplete and wrong. We intend to challenge it and spend money doing so. We intend to be present in the U.S. challenging it. I invite the Elon. Member to lift himself above petty partisan politics and join us in trying to protect the future of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister for International Trade. This morning the Prime Minister, in one of his musing interviews, said it may not be the right interpretation that we would have a binding mechanism-that may not be the way it appears when it is put down on paper.
Is the Prime Minister shifting ground once again on what our demands are in the negotiations? Have we changed our position? Are we now saying we do not necessarily want a binding mechanism for trade disputes?

Mr. Speaker, the Premier of Ontario, after being briefed by the trade negotiators, has clearly indicated that matters of government procurement are no longer part of the negotiation package accepted by the Americans. Have we now
once again shifted our ground from the expectations put forward to the Canadian people?

speakeroldname: Hon. Pat Carney (Minister for International Trade):

No,
Mr. Speaker, we have not shifted and we are not confused. As far as Premier Peterson is concerned, he knows very well that the bulk of the new jobs created by the free trade agreement, estimated by the Economic Council at 40 per cent, would be in Ontario. It is in Ontario's interest to have a free trade agreement.
But you do not have a comprehensive free trade agreement.
It will be comprehensive.
Oh, yes!
It will not be sectoral. It will meet the needs of Canadians across the country.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I have before me a letter of February 12, 1987, from the Prime Minister where he promised continuous and unbroken participation by the Government of Newfoundland and Labrador in the talks between Canada and France over the fishery dispute. What is the point of continuous and unbroken participation if the Government of Canada consistently ignores the position of the Government and people of Newfoundland and Labrador?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we do not consistently ignore the advice and representations of the Government and people and industry of Newfoundland. We have made arrangements, which I think are unparalleled in Canadian history, to involve the Government of Newfoundland, the fishermen of Newfoundland, and the industry of Newfoundland in the negotiations. They have been present for the last several months. They were in Paris for the negotiations which took place last weekend. The Premier of Newfoundland decided to withdraw, I hope temporarily, from those negotiations.
The Government of Canada has an obligation to proceed to try to establish an arrangement that will serve the interests of the fishing industry and the fishermen of Newfoundland, whatever the attitude of the Premier of Newfoundland regarding participation. I invite him back. The negotiations are going on and they would be better with his presence than with his absence.
September 18, 1987

Mr. Speaker, how can these talks continue without the Government breaking its promise of continuous and full participation? Why does the Government not halt the talks, sit down with the Government of Newfoundland and Labrador, and come up with an acceptable position before it goes back to the negotiations?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the letter quoted was an undertaking by the Prime Minister of Canada to do everything we can to ensure continuous participation by the Government of Newfoundland and others concerned. We are doing everything we can. We have involved them fully in briefings prior to the negotiations. We took them with us to Paris. They are welcome to be with us at the negotiations which will continue later on in Ottawa. Our commitment to having Newfoundland involved is continuous.
I repeat: This is going to be a very important decision if we achieve a negotiated settlement. It is in the interests of the Government of Newfoundland to have its Premier there. We hope he will accept the outstanding invitation of the Government of Canada to continue to play his part. We hope he will not follow the NDP line which is always to walk away.

STATEMENT MADE BY MINISTER OF FISHERIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Fisheries said in this House on January 28 that:
Our commitment to the people of Newfoundland and Labrador is that any
price which is too high for Newfoundland and Labrador is too high for
Canada.
By its actions the Government has now taken the position that it knows what is best for Newfoundland and not the Government and people of Newfoundland. Is that not the highest form of unbelievable arrogance by the Government of this country?

Mr. Speaker, it is a matter of record that the Government wants the entire boundary dispute on the East Coast of Canada to go to a third party, the International Court of Justice in the Hague, as soon as possible. That is according to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans.
My question is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Why did Canada go along, without a murmur of protest, when this week in the United Nations France nominated its own chief negotiator in the Canada-France fishing talks to sit as a judge on this very same International Court of Justice? Is that not a little like inviting the hangman to sit on the jury?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again the answer, known to everyone interested in facts rather than rhetoric, is no, that is not at all the situation.
I am not sure, but perhaps the Hon. Member can tell us when he rises, why the Liberal Party, with its presumed interest in this question, did not lead on the question of the fishery in Newfoundland, as the walk-away New Democratic Party led on the question-
We just walk away in the polls.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Excuse me, the walk-away violently NDP.
The answer with respect to the court is that Mr. Guillaume, if he is chosen to the court, will be prohibited by well known practices to sit on any case in which he has been in any way involved.

Mr. Speaker, Canada's new strategy is to negotiate with the French so they can fish for codfish even outside the disputed zone on the East Coast of Canada while the entire boundary dispute is sent to the International Court where the chief French negotiator sits as a judge. Boy, do we have the French on the ropes now!
Does the Minister not realize that the fishery this year is very poor and there is not enough for our own fishermen and their families, let alone negotiating the French fleet to enter our territory? How does he rationalize doing that, when his own Government has appointed a commission of inquiry that is investigating why the cod resource is so depleted on the east coast of Canada?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):

Mr. Speaker, there is a melange of accusation, as well as the assertion of a couple of rather unique Liberal Party principles. One is that any negotiation should be carried out here on the floor of the House of Commons, telegraphing

September 18, 1987
Oral Questions
everything we are doing to the people with whom we are negotiating, rather than carrying it out so that it might come to a successful conclusion within the negotiating concept.
The second idea is even more breathtaking. agent with the CNTU in Quebec. Given the strong criticisms expressed by CNTU, QFL and CEQ officials concerning this dangerous infiltration of labour unions in Quebec, can the Minister assure the House that there is no source or agent of CSIS in Quebec unions or elsewhere, and especially that they never did act as agents provocateurs in the Quebec labour movement?

speakeroldname: Hon. James Kelleher (Solicitor General of Canada):
subtopic: UNION INFILTRATION BY CSIS AGENTS-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I have already advised the House, first, CSIS does not target labour unions because they are labour unions. That is not within our mandate. In addition to that, I asked the Osbaldeston committee-you will see it quite clearly in their mandate-to look at this whole matter of targeting and the whole matter of recruiting sources, and the whole matter of defining more clearly the roles between counter-subversion and lawful dissent. I believe I am carrying out my duties as Solicitor General under the Act in a careful and prudent way.

The first is that the announcement from Washington today is accepted and welcomed by all of us in the House of Commons as a very important step forward, and I am sure that Members of the House of Commons would want to endorse and be associated with the congratulations that the Prime
September 18, 1987

Minister is conveying to both President Reagan and Secretary General Gorbachev.

subsubtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF U.S.-U.S.S.R. ARMS CONTROL AGREEMENT-VERIFICATION OF NUCLEAR TESTS

Second, as the Hon. Member so astutely pointed out, one of the surprising and important developments is that there has been an agreement, after an eight-year hiatus, to resume discussions on nuclear testing. That brings directly to the fore the importance of verification in which Canada has some very real expertise. That expertise will be available fully if it can be put into service.
Finally, I know that Members of the House will want to be brought up to date as fully as possible with what in fact has been discussed and decided in Washington, and what the next steps might be. I have, consequently, spoken this morning to the Chairman of the Standing Committee on External Affairs and International Trade to propose that, as a first step in ensuring that Parliament is fully informed, I would be prepared to make my senior officials available for a full in camera briefing relating to all of the information we have with regard to the nature of the agreement and subsequent steps. Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Deputy Prime Minister. It concerns Air-India 182. The Minister will know that various officials of the federal Government, and the federal Government, are being sued by Air-India for $120 million. Air-India alleges in its Statement of Claim that the destruction of its aircraft with the consequent loss of life was due to the negligence of the defendants some of whom were federal government officials.
In paragraph 30 of its Statement of Claim Air-India indicates: "In the months of May and June 1985, the existence of circumstances posing a threat to Air-India's operations was brought to the knowledge of all the defendants in the form of letters and verbal communications from the plaintiff'. Air-India is making a very serious allegation. It is suggesting that the federal Government is somehow negligent and responsible for the destruction of Air-India 182 because it prewarned the Government of Canada, or officials of the Government of Canada, by way of letters and verbal communications.
In view of the very serious allegations made in the Statement of Claim filed in the Supreme Court of Ontario and with the Federal Court of Canada, will the Deputy Prime Minister, on behalf of the Government of Canada, now initiate a full and
Oral Questions
complete judicial enquiry into the circumstances surrounding the destruction of Air-India 182?

Member may have a different opinion from this Minister, it is our opinion, and that of the Department of Justice, that we cannot discuss the case because it is before the courts.

Mr. Speaker, as you know we have had a Royal Commission inquiry into the Hinton rail disaster, another into the Ocean Ranger disaster. We had a Royal Commission inquiry into the conduct of a Minister of the Crown. There were lawsuits launched in two of those situations. Those lawsuits did not preclude a Royal Commission inquiry.

In view of the tragic loss of life-329 people were murdered in the Air-India tragedy-in view of the allegations that there were advance warnings to the federal Government, and in view of the allegations that the federal Government may in fact have been in some way responsible, does the Deputy Prime Minister not believe it is time now to have a Royal Commission inquiry into all the circumstances surrounding the destruction of Air-India 182, and to look also into the conduct of various federal Government officials and the conduct of various Ministers of the Crown at the time?

subsubtopic: POSITION OF UNITED STATES PRESIDENT-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
What will the Government be doing, apart from buying American advertising, on the matter on acid rain? And what does the Government intend to do to convince the U.S. President of the need for a drastic reduction in acid-rain-causing emissions? What effective measures will he take to convince the President?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: POSITION OF UNITED STATES PRESIDENT-GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 very much appreciate the subject and the tone of the question!
We have already taken a major step because we have here in this House a statement from the President of the United States on the matter of acid rain. It is the first time we get such a position and we now have an obligation and a duty to make sure that the President and not a scientific group is speaking on behalf of the United States.
Secondly, the report that has just come out in the United States purports to be based on scientific evidence. Canadian scientists are absolutely not in agreement with the conclusions, and on a scientific basis we intend to question the findings of the American panel.
Of course there will be many other measures, and hopefully we can count on the co-operation of the Hon. Member and her party as well as other parties in this House, in order to be sure that Canada is protected against the threat of acid rain.

Mr. Speaker, while I welcome the statement as far as it goes, I would ask the Minister if he does not admit that perhaps the Canadian Government itself has been sending out a mixed message, for example, in accepting the joint envoys' report, which was a very complacent one? Of course, it has been getting a mixed message in reply from the American President. What is the Government going to do to ensure that we have a consistent message on acid rain getting out there, and that it gets right to the top?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have brought the message right to
the top on several occasions. We have done it more effectively and assiduously than it had ever been done before. We also have an undertaking, what we consider to be an undertaking, from the President of the United States himself. We believe it is the President who speaks for the United States, not some groups of scientists which might be put together as a result of an act of Congress.
That is not to say that we do not have a problem. We have a very major problem regarding the commitment of the United States to accept the scientific evidence and to get on with the fight against acid rain. We are going to continue to press them at the highest levels. I will raise it with Secretary Shultz. The Prime Minister will continue to raise it with President Reagan. The Minister of the Environment has already been in touch, after the so-called report which was issued the other day, with his counterpart in the United States. We look forward to extensive co-operation, Member of Parliament to Congressmen, Senator-if I may use that word-to Senator, to try to ensure that Canada's message is received as effectively and pervasively as possible.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 10, 1987, the Prime Minister, with respect to the Canada-France negotiations, said in the House: "We hope that the ultimate negotiations will meet with the complete satisfaction of the Newfoundland fishermen whose interests we are deeply committed to protecting". The Minister of Fisheries said on January 28: "If in the process, the demands of France exceed that which Canadian fishermen and Atlantic Governments can support, there will be no agreement".
The last time I checked, Newfoundland was an Atlantic Province, her Government an Atlantic Government. It has said no to the position put forward by Canada in Paris last weekend. In light of the commitments of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Fisheries, stated fully and openly in this House, I ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs how the Government can continue with negotiations as scheduled in October when the Canadian negotiating team, that is, the federal Government and all of the Atlantic Provinces, have not reached a consensus on a Canadian position to be put before the French in the October negotiations?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is quite helpful that the Hon. Member has read into the record those statements made by my Prime Minister and by my colleague, the Minister of Fisheries. They do represent the position of the Government of Canada. They are the reason why we broke all precedent and went ahead and established for the first time, I believe, in history,
September 18, 1987

this kind of full participation in an international negotiation that rests technically and legally within the domain of the Government of Canada.
Newfoundland has been present, up until Saturday night when, on instructions from its Premier, its representative left a portion of the discussions. We regret that decision. We hope that Newfoundland will come back.
Newfoundland has been kept fully advised of what the Canadian position was going to be.
For how long?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The Hon. Member asks me for how long. I would have to verify for how long, but certainly, to speak of the events that have given rise to recent developments, certainly since the counsel, Mr. Fortier, carried out his consultations preparatory to the negotiations in France.
We have been trying to bring the provinces in. We brought the industry in. We brought the fishermen in. We brought them into a matter, into a negotiation which, strictly speaking, is our business. We know it is too important to hide behind jurisdictions. We want to have the best possible solution for all Canadians. We hope that the Government of Newfoundland will want the best possible solution, too. It can guarantee that much more by being present than it can by walking away.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian Tobin (Humber-Port au Port-St. Barbe):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I say to the Secretary of State for External Affairs that, strictly speaking, these negotiations are the business of every Atlantic Government and the business of every fisherman who makes his living from the sea in the Atlantic and not just the business of the Government of Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Communications
speechtext: He just finished saying that.

I remind the Secretary of State that the Government entered into a process in which it committed itself to the principle that, if a position was put and a demand was made by France that exceeded the agreement of the provinces and if any province disagreed with the demand put and the negotiating position of the federal Government, no deal would be made.
Is the Secretary of State telling us that the Government of Canada, having done a mea culpa and having given an apology in the House of Commons last January for its early behind-the-back-door agreement, has now changed its position and is prepared to make a treaty with France notwithstanding the views of Newfoundland or any other Atlantic province? Is he telling us that there has been a change on the part of the Prime Minister and the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have two comments, if I might. The
Oral Questions
first is that the Hon. Member quite properly drew attention to the fact that there is a brand new process here. We are not hiding behind jurisdiction. It is a process that was not in place under Liberal Governments. When Liberal Governments negotiated they shut everybody out. We are not shutting people out because that results in bad agreements. We have plenty of proof of that. We are trying to get a good agreement that will last, which is why we have brought the Government of Newfoundland, the industry of Newfoundland, and the fishermen of Newfoundland into the process.
Is the new process still in place, yes or no?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The Hon. Member asks whether or not a position has changed. Our position has not changed. The position of the Government of Newfoundland has changed for the moment in that the Premier has decided to absent himself from these discussions. We hope he comes back.

subsubtopic: HONDURAS AND BOLIVIA-INTRODUCTION OF VISA REQUIREMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Employment and Immigration. On September 1 of this year 1 asked the Minister whether he would consider imposing a visa requirement on Honduras considering the increasing number of Hondurans coming to Canada; particularly to Vancouver, claiming refugee status. It has become clear over the past two weeks that some of those Hondurans have been counselled by travel agents in Honduras to use the refugee system to claim entry to Canada rather than the regular immigration system. Indeed, they have been given false expectations about what would happen when they come to Canada.
Two weeks have passed. Can the Minister advise the House if he is prepared to proceed with imposing a visa requirement on Honduras, first to protect Hondurans from being taken advantage of and, most important, to ensure that our refugee system in Canada is not compromised or unduly burdened?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
subsubtopic: HONDURAS AND BOLIVIA-INTRODUCTION OF VISA REQUIREMENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, two weeks ago we told the Hon. Member that we will consider the case of some countries from which we face problems in terms of refugee claimants. We have considered two particular cases in this regard, Honduras and Bolivia. Over the last nine months we have received 1,000 migrants from Honduras claiming refugee status and 300 from Bolivia. Accordingly, we decided as of midnight last night that visa requirements will be imposed on Honduras and Bolivia.
