subsubtopic: DEATH OF YUGOSLAV REFUGEE IN CALGARY-REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Solicitor General and it concerns Damir Durekovic, who was originally from Yugoslavia. He was a real political refugee who came to Canada in 1984. Tragically, his body was found last week in Calgary.
I wish to quote from his refugee examination hearing held on June 28, 1984: "The basis of his application was that he feared for his life as his father, also a refugee in West Germany, was murdered in July, 1983. Mr. Durekovic claimed that the murder was politically motivated due to the fact that his father had authored five books which were critical of the Yugoslav regime". The Croation community in Canada is very upset.
I wish to ask the Solicitor General if he will order a full and complete investigation into this tragic death.

speakeroldname: Hon. James Kelleher (Solicitor General of Canada):
subsubtopic: DEATH OF YUGOSLAV REFUGEE IN CALGARY-REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Hon. Member was good enough to bring this to my attention by way of a letter, part of which he has quoted today. I was glad to be able to assist him in some small way. I asked my officials to look into this matter immediately and see what was happening.
I have now been advised by my officials that the Calgary police force are conducting an investigation, that it is a continuing investigation, and at this time it is under the purview and jurisdiction of the Solicitor General of Alberta.
If the Hon. Member has further facts to give me which may not be known to them, I will be happy to receive those facts and pass them on to the appropriate authorities.

subsubtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR TOBACCO GROWERS-APPLICATION OF RULES IN ONTARIO
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Agriculture. He will know that last winter Agriculture Canada allotted $30 million to aid tobacco producers in the Provinces of Ontario, Quebec, and Prince Edward Island, in order that they could exit the industry or switch to alternate crops.
I wish to ask the Minister why the arrangement that was negotiated with the Government of Prince Edward Island which changed its targets is more flexible than that drawn up with Ontario where the rules and bureaucracy have added to the tobacco growers' frustrations instead of helping them to address the surplus problem.
Oral Questions

subsubtopic: ASSISTANCE FOR TOBACCO GROWERS-APPLICATION OF RULES IN ONTARIO
speechtext:
I appreciate the question of the Hon. Member. He must realize that in the tobacco reduction program, like many other areas, the Government has had to break new ground.
We sat down with the various provinces and the producer groups within each province and signed specific agreements that were unique and peculiar to situations.
The agreement with Ontario requires revision. The take-up is not as high as I would like it to be. Last week I met with representatives of the tobacco marketing board. I have requested that my provincial counterpart meet with the tobacco board, possibly as early as next week, for the purpose of reviewing the progress to date with the thought of relaxing the requirements in order that there can be a greater take-up in the Ontario program.

subsubtopic: UNIVERSAL ACCESS TO FAIR ORAL HEARINGS BEFORE REFUGEE BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my honour and duty to present a petition on behalf of a number of residents of the City of Toronto who object to Bill C-55. The petitioners feel that it will have the effect of preventing refugees from reaching our borders, or if they reach our borders, they will be turned away without their claim being properly heard.
They also object to the concept of a safe country which has no foundation in law. They point out that a better system was proposed nearly two years ago by the standing committee of Parliament.
Therefore, they pray and call upon Parliament to ensure that Government and Parliament will withdraw Bill C-55 and substitute the sort of legislation for which the standing committee asked two years ago, and in duty bound your petitioners will ever pray.

subsubtopic: OPPOSITION TO DISCONTINUATION OF CN RAIL SERVICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is both an honour and a privilege for me to present a petition signed by 200 residents of my Glengarry-Prescott-Russell riding who are strongly urging the Federal Government and this Parliament to make sure that the CN Rail service between Ottawa and Montreal, and also between Ottawa and Sudbury continue to operate and does not disappear as provided in an internal document of CN Rail.

subsubtopic: UNIVERSAL ACCESS TO FAIR ORAL HEARINGS BEFORE REFUGEE BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour and duty to present a petition signed by a number of Canadian citizens from St. John's, Newfoundland and Vancouver and Surrey, British Columbia. They humbly petition the House to show that Bill C-55 will result in many, and perhaps most, refugees who reach our borders being turned away without having their claim heard on the merits of their case.
Therefore, the undersigned petitioners humbly pray and call upon Parliament to ensure that Government and Parliament withdraw Bill C-55 and substitute legislation embodying the principles of fair and quick oral hearings of claims of refugee claimants before a refugee board independent of the Immigration Commission, universal access to such hearings for every
September 18, 1987

applicant in Canada, and the right to appeal on the basis of fact.

subsubtopic: SAFETY OF REAR SEAT AUTOMOBILE PASSENGERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour for me to present a petition signed by residents of Brantford (Ontario), Lethbridge (Alberta), Lindsay (Ontario), Aylmer (Quebec) and Ottawa.
The petitioners are asking for changes to be made to the highway safety regulation. They believe that rear seatbelts are now inadequate and that the sufferings of highway collision victims could be greatly reduced or avoided. They believe also that the costs of medical care could be also reduced and eliminated.
For these reasons and many others, Mr. Speaker, they are asking Parliament to agree to make compulsory the installation of three-point adjustable safety belts for rear seat passengers, and also the installation of inflatable bags at the front of cars.

For these reasons and many more, the petitioners humbly pray and call upon Parliament to increase assistance immediately for emergency shelter and co-operative housing.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S. O. 29 CANADA-FRANCE AGREEMENT-FISHING RIGHTS
speechtext:
The Chair received notice of the application of the Hon. Member for St. John's East (Mr. Harris) who has raised a matter which is of very great concern to him, to other Hon. Members from the Province of Newfoundland and Labrador, and to all Canadians.
The House will remember that some time ago there was an emergency debate on this issue. The Hon. Member of course would urge that there has been a recent event, as a consequence of which certain persons representing the Province of Newfoundland and Labrador apparently are not, at least for the moment, with the Canadian negotiating team. The Hon. Member is concerned about that, as I am sure are all Hon. Members, and has urged upon the Chair that the House be adjourned to debate this matter on an urgent basis this afternoon.
I want to assure the Hon. Member for St. John's East that the Chair has given it very careful consideration. I feel that under the circumstances perhaps it is not necessary to go ahead with an emergency debate this afternoon.
However, I want the Hon. Member to know that the entire issue is taken seriously by the Chair, as I know it is by other Hon. Members.

September 18, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976

The House proceeded to the consideration of Bill C-55, an Act to amend the Immigration Act, 1976 and to amend other Acts in consequence thereof, as reported (with amendments) from a legislative committee.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
It is my obligation to make a ruling in the House in respect of amendments to Bill C-55, an Act to amend the Immigration Act, 1976 and to amend other Acts in consequence thereof.
I think I should begin by pointing out to the House and to the listening and watching public that there are 77 motions on the Notice Paper in amendment to Bill C-55. I have examined these motions and will allow debate to proceed on the motions which are acceptable at this time.
I want Hon. Members to know that the majority of these amendments were received late yesterday, and I want to congratulate the staff of the Journals and the Public Bills Offices for the long hours they put in in preparing the motions and the material to brief me this morning. I know that some of our officials were working until 5 a.m. this day in order to give me the briefing I need so that the convenience of all Hon. Members is properly met.
Motions Nos. 2 and 3 will be debated and voted on separately-
Motions Nos. 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 13, and 14 are attempts to amend Clause 14 of the Bill. They will be grouped together for debate, with a vote on Motion No. 13 first. An affirmative vote on Motion No. 13 obviates the necessity for a vote on the remainder of the group. However, a negative vote on Motion No. 13 requires separate votes on Motions Nos. 4, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, and 14.
Motions Nos. 15, 25, 26, 28, 31, 32, 33, 35 and 36 will be grouped for debate and voted on separately. All of these motions deal with the concept of a credible basis for refugee claims.
Motions Nos. 18 and 21 will be debated together with an affirmative vote on Motion No. 18 obviating the question being put on Motion No. 21. A negative vote on Motion No. 18 will require the question to be put on Motion No. 21. Motions Nos. 27, 29 and 34 will be debated together but voted upon separately.
I want to advise Hon. Members that the Chair will return to the House with a more definitive ruling as soon as possible.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Government House Leader); Minister of State (Treasury Board); Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not speaking to your ruling, but I just want to make a point and indicate a position in the event that I may not be in the House when it comes up.
It is my understanding that there are amendments on the Order Paper presented by the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi) who is unavoidably detained today. There has been a request from the Official Opposition that the amendments in his name be moved by another Member. We have considered this matter; we have considered it in the light of Standing Order 114(10) which points out that report stage is there to provide Members who are not Members of the committee with an opportunity to have the House consider specific amendments they wish to propose. It also goes on to say that it is not meant to be a reconsideration of the committee stage of the Bill.
I point out that the amendments that are on the Order Paper were tabled in committee, but only one was moved by the Hon. Member at clause by clause stage. I impute no motives in this but the Government is content to have these motions moved by the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia), I believe.
I would draw your attention, Mr. Speaker, to Standing Order 114(10) which in part reads:
NOTE: The Speaker will not normally select for consideration by the
House any motion previously ruled out of order in committee and will
normally only select. motions which were not or could not be presented in
committee.
I make that point and indicate in the spirit of having debate on the amendments that-we are naturally prepared to have any amendments which the Chair finds to hp in order moved by the Hon. Member ipr Davenport rather thap the Hon. Member for York West.
I do ask the Chair to consider the spirit of parliamentary reform, the spirit of the legislative committee, the spirit of the discussion, of the hearing of witnesses and the clause by clause consideration in committee where the whole purpose of clause by clause discussion is to have ample time to discuss it, and ease the work of this House, since we do have several committees sitting at one time, by placing amendments at committee and endeavouring to have them either talked out, passed or not. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, to consider that in your ruling.
I indicate formally that the Government is prepared to allow those amendments that you find to be in order standing on the Order Paper in the name of the Hon. Member for York West moved by the Hon. Member for Davenport.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Calgary South (Mr. Hawkes) on the same point of order?

Yes, Mr. Speaker. It is a follow-up in the same vein. Seldom have I been on a legislative committee that spent so many hours hearing public testimony or that made so many amendments to a Bill. I think it speaks to the complexity of this Bill. We also chose in that committee to group items, I think in a way similar to the way you have grouped them for us today, but we took things out of sequence.

September 18, 1987

I would like to bring to your attention that at about five o'clock on Friday, September 11, we negatived two amendments in committee known as N-4-17 and N-4-27. I think you will find that they are identical to Motion No. 2 which is before us this afternoon. Perhaps you would like to have a little more time to examine the record and those two particular amendments, Mr. Speaker, and that it might be wiser for us to begin the debate this afternoon on Motion No. 3.
I would also suggest that throughout the course of dealing with the 77 amendments, from time to time some input from Members of the House who were actually in committee could be helpful in organizing ourselves as we proceed.

Mr. Speaker, my point of order relates to the fact that in the same session of Parliament, Parliament should not pronounce upon the same issues. My distinct impression is that many of the issues dealt with in Bill C-84 are being dealt with in Bill C-55. Is my understanding of that situation correct? Should we be pronouncing upon a number of issues which appear to many people to have been touched upon in an earlier Bill passed in the same session of Parliament?

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Two points of order have been raised in the last few minutes, one by the Minister of State (Mr. Lewis), and one by the Hon. Member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Kilgour). As I indicated to the House, the ruling that I have made is the first ruling; I will be returning to the House as soon as possible with respect to the remainder of the matters that must be decided.
It would be possible to go ahead at this time with Motion No. 3, while perhaps I have some time to consider the matter raised with respect to Motion No. 2. That might be the easiest way to approach things. If that met with the approval of the House I would suggest that that is how we proceed for now.
The Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) has a point of order. I have not been ignoring him. I now have a chance to recognize him and give him the floor.

Mr. Speaker, my point relates to what was said by the Hon. Minister of State (Mr. Lewis), and the Hon. Member for Calgary South (Mr. Hawkes) about the work done in committee.
First, I wish very sincerely to congratulate the staff of Journals, the Clerks and the Speaker on their hard and speedy work. I wish to thank the staff of Journals and the Clerks for their assistance in recent days and weeks. Their work has been vital.
I wish to comment on the point which the Minister rightly raised, that our plan is to give people ample time, as the Minister puts it, in committee to consider all these matters. Well, Mr. Speaker, there wasn't ample time. I wish to draw the attention of the Speaker and the Members to a problem, in that cases like this may warrant some administrative action or possibly a reconsideration of some parts of our rules of order, particularly the one that provides that debate on the report
Immigration Act, 1976
shall begin within 48 hours of it being tabled. If it does not require it, it seems to provide for that. Although that measure was relaxed for a day this time, the situation this week has brought to a head rather extraordinary circumstances.
The committee's work was extraordinarily heavy. It worked for 55 hours in six days and dealt with 30 groups of witnesses, sometimes as many as four in a group, and as many as 10 witnesses in one day. Then for three days it did the clause-byclause work on all the clauses in a Bill that is 62 pages long. The report of the committee was also fairly lengthy.
A few interim copies of the Bill as amended were available on Wednesday. The regular copies of the amended Bill were not available until after 10 a.m. Thursday. That was when debate would supposedly have begun. There were differences in line and page numbering between the interim and regular copies of the Bill which caused a good many extra hours of work in my office and I believe also in the Clerk's and Journals offices as well.
The fact is that this Bill was unusually long, unusually complex and unusually controversial. It required many carefully worked out amendments, not all of which could have been put in committee, even if there had been more time, because some amendments are consequent upon other amendments moved by other Parties in the committee. Even the Government, I believe, with all its extra staff, needed this extra day.
I am grateful for the extra day that was allowed but I would draw the attention of the House to this problem which does not occur with a Bill that has only two or three clauses or is only two or three pages long, but can occur in a case like this. I think these cases are not provided for well enough by the rules, and I would hope that it may be possible to speed up the production of the Bill as amended by committee or that the Standing Orders may give a wider discretion to allow for more time between the depositing of the report and the beginning of the debate. There has not been ample time and I regret that very much. When a very controversial, large and complex Bill is to be debated in future, I hope more time will be given both in committee and between the committee finishing and the report being debated.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Hon. Member for York West (Mr. Marchi) who has been ably watching this Bill go through committee, I would also like to express our appreciation for what has been done by the staff and by everyone involved. I would suggestion that Motion No. 2, which happens to have been proposed by the Chairman of the committee, is one that ought to stand on its own merits and ought to be debated at report stage. It is a complex motion and it deserves to be dealt with by way of normal proceedings, as other motions will be debated, motions which are already printed along with Motion No. 2 on the notice paper.

September 18, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
As far as we are concerned, we could start by debating Motion No. 3 as you have already ruled and we are prepared to do so.

On a point of order, Mr. Speaker. 1 see that there is some disagreement to start the debate with Motion No. 2.
This motion stands in my name. In passing, I would like to thank the Journals Branch staff for spending last night, until five in the morning, preparing these 77 amendment motions. A lot of these motions arrived late yesterday, at five or six o'clock.
One thing that I would like to point out to my collegues in this House is that I have had no opportunity to speak on Bill C-55. I have been democratically elected to represent my constituents, and I believe that I should be allowed to explain why I have introduced certain amendments. 1 believe that this is my right and privilege. All of the amendments which I introduced are for the good of Bill C-55, the good of the Canadian people and the good of my constituency.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: l want to thank Hon. Members for their consideration while 1 consider the matters raised by the various points of order including the comments about Motion No. 2. I might indicate to the Hon. Member for La Prairie (Mr. Jourdenais) that the Chair of course will carefully consider his intervention and his remarks. In the meantime, 1 take it that it is the disposition of the House to accept my suggestion that we proceed with debate on Motion No. 3.

Motion No. 3.
That Bill C-55, be amended in Clause 9
(a)	by striking out lines 46 and 47 at page 7 and substituting the following therefor:
"two weeks after the making of the order; or"
(b)	by striking out line 2 at page 8 and substituting the following therefore: "required to leave Canada, and in any case not less than two weeks after the
notice is received."
He said: Mr. Speaker, this motion deals with one of the many little points in this Bill which make it not so much a means of admitting refugees as a means of keeping people out of Canada, some of whom may be refugees. It is a complex system that has been constructed. It reflects the work of some public servants over a period of half a dozen years and the earnest desire of some senior public servants in the Immigration Department.
Clause 9 concerns one of limitations to be placed upon a person who has arrived in Canada and is claiming refugee status. The clause provides that while a person is to have legal representation, he is limited in getting it. He can have a lawyer but only within some limitations. The preferred system is that he have a lawyer who is paid by the Minister.
I think the Supreme Court would look in a rather strange way at having a person who is in a contest with the Minister, a
person who has been told that he has no right to be in Canada unless he can prove that he is a refugee, prove that he met the safe-country test, prove that he met the credibility test and go on to prove his claim, if he is lucky enough to get that far doing so with the help of a lawyer hired by the Minister in charge of putting him out of the country if he cannot prove it. That is not a very equal system. It is not a very good introduction for a person who, like many refugee claimants, might some day become a very fine citizen of Canada, as Rabbi Plaut keeps reminding us happened in his own case.
The Bill does allow that a person may get his or her own lawyer at his or her own expense, but the Bill wants to limit the time allowed for doing that. This particular provision appears at the bottom of page 7 of the Bill. It says he will have a lawyer appointed by the Minister unless he is represented by a barrister or solicitor who is available to take instructions with respect to such an application, in the case of a person against whom a removal order is made within 24 hours after making the order, or, in the case of a person to whom a departure notice is issued prior to the date on or before which the person is required to leave Canada.
In the normal experience in Canada getting a lawyer within 24 hours is often next to impossible. Getting through with a phone call to a lawyer may be next to impossible. There are competent lawyers. Most of them are not unemployed. Most of them do not regularly work, for example, on weekends, or they are not necessarily in their offices available on statutory holidays when these things may happen. If they are reachable by telephone they cannot necessarily drop whatever they are doing and that very day go out to interview a client. If they have an appearance in court scheduled for that day, it is a very grave matter not to appear. If they have an appointment with a client scheduled for that day, it may be a very grave matter to the client if it is cancelled. In fact, we have had complaints from the immigration department about lawyers who cancel their appearances for one reason or another.
What is envisaged here is that the only lawyer who might be available to this person as his lawyer of choice would have to be one who is in effect unemployed that day. It is very unreasonable. The Supreme Court has said that even a nonCanadian, someone who has come to Canada and said he is a refugee and needs the protection of Canada from the country persecuting him, is entitled to due process. That includes reasonable access to legal counsel. This is not reasonable access. It takes time to contact the lawyer. It takes time for the lawyer to act within his schedule or refer a person to another lawyer who might have time more immediately.
When the lawyer does arrive, it takes time to prepare a case on which the future of that person may depend. If the person fails at the coming inquiry for which he is to be prepared, he will not get any hearing of his refugee claim. If he is told that
September 18, 1987

he came from a safe country, that is a country considered safe in terms of this law, even if he feels the decision is mistaken in his case and that it is not safe for him, he may be sent back there.
If he passes that test but does not convince two people in that preliminary screening that he has what they call a credible basis for his claim, mainly based not on his evidence but, as the Act lays it out, on evidence they have, prior to meeting with him, in other words a preconceived opinion depending on which country it is he says was persecuting him, he has to make that case. He has to instruct his lawyer and that is not necessarily quickly and easily done, particularly in the case of a genuine refugee.
If he is a phoney, perhaps he will have a case already made, a lawyer already arranged, et cetera, and things will go smoothly. If he is a genuine refugee on the run for his life, perhaps having had to run through more than one country to find safety, he will be nervous, and afraid of officialdom. He may not know the details of our law.
The details of this law extend to 62 pages. Very few Canadians have even read the Bill, let alone claim to understand it. I suspect few Members of Parliament have read it, let alone claim to understand it. Yet this person has to face all the details of this Bill and he is supposed to get his lawyer within a day. That is in the case of a person against whom a removal order has been made or in the case of a person to whom a departure notice is issued. He has to do it on or before the day on which he is required to leave Canada. It is unnecessary and unreasonable to require such haste when we recognize that we may be dealing with a person who is in genuine danger of his life or liberty and is having some difficulty in speaking out.
We heard an excellent brief from the Women and Law Group who reminded us that not all refugees are men. Women refugees are subject to rather specialized forms of trouble to which men refugees are not. Women refugees have often experienced rape and other forms of sexual harassment by the people from whom they fled, border guards through whom they passed, security guards or jail guards where they were detained in different countries, and so on. It is not, so they told us and I take their word for it, easy for a woman in such a case to blurt out those facts to the first person in Canada who says, tell me all about it. It is the experience of competent lawyers who have years of experience dealing with cases of genuine refugees and who are respected by the courts of this country, that it may take some hours or even days of careful and skilled and sympathetic interviewing to bring out the essential facts of the story.
The present chairman of the Immigration Appeal Board gave us a case in point where a person went all the way through the process and only at the last, and because of a question from the chairman, said the reason he came on the run is because his father was killed in his home country. That was verified and that made the case, but he had not said it
Immigration Act, 1976
before because it is not easy to tell those things in all cases the first time.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: 1 am sorry, I must interrupt the Hon. Member because his time has expired.

Madam Speaker, we encountered this amendment in committee with one different word. I think the amendment then was that the period of time be extended for seven days. It now is for 14 days.
I think it is important to understand just how great an improvement this proposed system is with respect to protecting the rights of legitimate refugees compared to what is in place today. If the House were to adopt none of the report stage amendments, we would still have a system that would be the finest in the world. With some of the report stage amendments, I think it would be better still.
Members have to realize that what is happening to the administrative side is that humanitarian and compassionate concerns which are permissible in the Immigration Act will be considered prior to the commencement of an inquiry. If they are relevant, the person will be landed, and if they want to make a claim for refugee status, they can do it in what is called "in-status", inside the country.
When we talk about a removal order or departure notice, we are dealing with a brand new system under Bill C-55 that provides a barrister or solicitor to a refugee claimant, at taxpayers' expense, from the moment they indicate to the inquiry officer that they intend to make a claim. When a claimant formally makes a claim at an inquiry, it is adjourned immediately in order to provide that claimant with counsel. The Bill requires that when the decision is made for a removal or departure notice, reasons must be given and the lawyer must be present with the claimant.
A removal or departure order means that the claim to refugee status has been rejected. This provision of the Bill does not deal with people who still have a claim to refugee status, and certainly not with people who are determined to be refugees. It deals primarily with those thousands of people who have come to this country in the last couple of years to abuse our generosity and were found to be ineligible as refugees. This Bill allows an appeal on leave to a higher court and permits the claimant to ask for a stay of execution of that removal order for a minimum of 24 hours. They are provided with a lawyer of their choice, and that 24 hours or longer can be used to instruct counsel to prepare a legal document for the higher court within 15 days.
I suggest to the Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) that there are probably 24,000 people in the backlog who, under this system, would receive removal orders or departure notices. I ask the Member why we would want people who are determined not to be refugees to stay in the country two weeks longer at taxpayers' expense.

September 18, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
We have a well deserved reputation for humanity and generosity toward legitimate refugee claimants. But this part of the legislation provides some of our generosity to people who we decide are not refugees. They are provided with counsel and can stay the removal order for 24 hours. There is no good legal reason why those 24,000 people should be given two weeks when most of them had no claim in the first instance. Surely we have gone the extra mile with a 24-hour stay of execution of the order and the provision of counsel at taxpayers' expense. That is going a long way for people who try to abuse our system. I believe we should use the expense that would be incurred by that two weeks for legitimate refugees rather than the abusers of the system.

Mr. Speaker, it is really difficult to deal with any particular provision of this Bill in isolation. I believe one has to view any particular section of the Bill within the context of the over-all thrust of the legislation.
It would be appropriate to comment on this motion by referring to some testimony that was given before the legislative committee. I have the testimony of Professor Angus from Osgoode Hall, who I understand is an expert in administrative law and procedure. He concluded his comments about the Bill by saying:
I think it is fatally flawed in a number of respects. It reflects a bill drafted by an administration task force which has taken an extreme position on one side: it has been opposed with extreme positions on the other side, and we have failed to define the middle ground. That troubles me very much, and 1 think it should trouble your committee.
He went on to say:
Reasonable compromise has worked well in the past in this nation of ours so that we do not reach the extremes. I think the consequences may be very substantial.
He also said:
There are individuals who feel genuinely betrayed by these provisions in terms of their participation leading up to Bill C-55.
A number of individuals most surely will, as a matter of conscience, pursue civil disobedience against the provisions of these two statutes. We are going to see an elevation of conflict in society as a result of these two Bills. There will be Charter challenges.
I think there is a very substantial prospect that many of these Charter challenges will proceed. It grieves me deeply that we are at this point of Bill C-55. It is a one-sided view of a very serious matter of international and national concern.
Again, an expert in the area of administrative law predicts that there will be Charter challenges to a Bill which he views as very extreme. He states that we must really study this provision.
I suggest that it is a travesty of justice when one requires a person who is subject to a removal order or departure notice to come up with a lawyer within 24 hours, when it may be a matter of life and death. It is a travesty of the fundamental principles that all Canadians believe in.
As well, the statement by the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) about dealing with humanitarian considerations prior to the process defies logic. One knows that
humanitarian considerations are those things that are raised in the last resort. They are matters that are brought up on an appeal to a Minister, on an appeal to the kind of group that has been charged with that responsibility, the special review committee. It involves people who go beyond the strict limits of the law and the strict procedures that are set down in our law to determine whether there may be any extenuating circumstances which justify giving a person an extra opportunity to be heard, or giving a person the benefit of the doubt.
Again, this question was dealt with in the hearings before the committee. The very distinguished lawyer, with many years of experience in immigration law and refugee law, Miss Barbara Jackman, appeared on behalf of the Canadian Bar Association and pointed out that senior immigration officers are enforcement officials. They are enforcement minded and their concern is removing people from Canada, not facilitating entry.
I support this amendment. I think it is an entirely reasonable amendment. This particular section of the Bill, the way it is currently drafted, will be subject to challenge. I really, quite frankly, cannot understand why the Government is proceeding with many of the provisions of this Bill. I do not understand why it is not willing to entertain amendments. As was mentioned by Professor Angus, if we have a Bill which is a response to an extreme position and which will be subject to Charter challenges from day one, we will not be getting the kind of process wanted by the Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. Weiner), all Members of this House and all Canadians. We will end up with a system that will become bogged down from day one. This is the overwhelming consensus expressed by many of the witnesses who appeared before the legislative committee.
I do support the amendment and I would hope the Minister of State for Immigration and his colleagues in this House would support this amendment as well, if they are indeed interested in arriving at a Bill which will improve the situation and give us a process that will work, not one which will not work.

Madam
Speaker, I too would like ask the House to support this amendment for the simple reason that I think it is really crucial as we look at what this Bill does. There has been a good intent on all sides of the House to try to resolve a very serious problem. However, I do think this Bill is too reactionary and too rigid. This particular amendment to the Bill will add a little fairness to the whole system.
What we are looking for is something that can expedite the whole process from a humane as well as from an efficient point of view. I think it is really important to recognize something the Hon. Member from Calgary was discussing, that is, the fact that these people had already been designated as not being credible refugees. I do not think that is right. This whole
September 18, 1987

process is in place so that it is part of the refugee designation process. It seems to me that because of the state of anxiety these people are in when entering a country under the conditions in which many refugees enter the country, it is really important that they be given the amount of time necessary for them to seek a solicitor. It seems to me that two weeks is not an over-extended amount of time when we know how slow the process has been in the past and when we know how difficult it has been, and that there are probably going to be challenges with respect to the Charter which will certainly cause all kinds of bottle-necks.
In the first instance, we recognize the fact that these people have not been designated as non-refugees or refugees at this point. That is why that process is in place. Surely we must give them full and adequate hearing. That cannot happen if they have to get a lawyer within 24 hours. Just imagine how we would feel, Madam Speaker, if we were in that state of anxiety, entering into a strange country, probably fleeing for our life and the lives of our family, and being told at that point that within 24 hours we must have a lawyer or face deportation. That is not fair or just and it is totally unreasonable.
If the amendment could be accepted, it would give a little more fairness to the Bill than what is there at the moment. I think it is a very unpalatable Bill because it certainly, as the previous speaker has said, puts the most extreme position forward. Certainly, the legislation is trying to kill a mosquito with a sledge-hammer.
Over and above that, I think we must always recognize the fact that we are in the process of refugee designation and at the first hearing the decision on refugee designation is not made. To be able to have a full and complete hearing with the solicitor is very important as one goes through that process. Expecting a potential refugee to be able to get a lawyer within 24 hours is very unreasonable.
I would urge Members on both sides of the House to support this amendment. It is a very small amendment but it certainly does add to the Bill a touch of humaneness and fairness. I think that is the kind of thing we are looking for. If we get the challenges with respect to the Charter as has been predicted, we know that huge bottle-necks will form in the system. If we can help the system to work expeditiously and be able to move people through whose lives are really threatened we should do so. In fact, I would suggest that the people who are under the deepest pressure, who probably are the real refugees, are the ones who are going to suffer the most without this amendment because they are the ones who will be incapable of finding a lawyer within 24 hours.
I think it is really important that we give these people a fair hearing, but we are not going to be able to do that if we expect them to appear themselves without counsel, or with counsel who is designated by the Government of Canada, within 24 hours, and that is about the only way they can proceed. I think
Immigration Act, 1976
it is really important that this type of amendment be supported. I would urge Members on both sides of the House to do so. We will certainly be supporting it.

Madam
Speaker, I will begin my remarks by doing something that is not done very often in this Chamber, that is, to compliment a member of the Opposition, the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap), who, during the committee process, of which I was part, showed day by day, hour by hour, during all 55 hours, his diligence, sincerity and, indeed, his good humour as we muddled through a very complicated and lengthy process.
The Member from the Liberal Party who spoke earlier, the Hon. Member for Laurier (Mr. Berger), had he been there, or had the Liberal critic been there on a regular basis, he would have been aware that during that process we moved the humanitarian aspects from the end of the process up towards the beginning. Therefore, it is indeed a much more humanitarian Bill. Counsel is, in most cases, already there, so the provision for the 24 hours very often is not required. The person can just turn to the counsel already provided.
We heard during the committee hearings from witness after witness that choice of counsel is very often used as a delaying tactic, mostly by those who have no respect for the system as it now stands. Indeed, those who may be considered most fraudulent or bogus among the refugee class are the ones who played with the system the most and who are still playing with the present system. Switching lawyers was often the way they did it. They would select a very prominent immigration lawyer who may or may not be available at the time of the hearing, and then when he was not available, there would be another delay. This would go on for months, if not years.
I also think there is a very important distinction to be made between counsel being paid by the Minister and being responsible to the Minister. Counsel is, indeed, paid for by the taxpayers of Canada. If I may be so bold, let me say that counsel is responsible to the taxpayers of Canada to ensure that justice is done under the laws of the land.
For these reasons, and the reasons brought forward by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes), I would urge that Motion No. 3 be defeated.

Madam Speaker, I, too, would like to take a moment in commending and thanking those members of the committee who worked so diligently through those 55 hours. We deeply appreciate, as do all Canadians, their efforts and, indeed, the quality of their work.
In response to the Hon. Member for Laurier (Mr. Berger) I would say that the committee represents a compromise between the views of many interveners at the committee and the concerns of the Government which gave rise to the Bill.

September 18, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
Professor Angus viewed a Bill that did not ensure that duty counsel would be a lawyer, and that did not provide the right, at inquiry, to represent himself or herself. The committee has responded to those areas of weakness in the Bill and the compromise would, in my view, satisfy Professor Angus, if not a number of other interveners.
The concerns of the Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr.Heap), and others, that many competent lawyers are not readily available is the reason that the Bill provides for duty counsel. The Government undertakes to ensure a maximum availability of competent lawyers, and the cost of those counsel will be borne by the Government.
The Government and the Minister have no interest in finding that a given claimant is not a refugee. If an error has been made, the Government has a public interest in correcting that error. When the error is not to the benefit of the claimant, the Minister would not want that error overlooked. Duty counsel, competent members of the bar, readily available at the expense of the Government, will ensure that the claimants can have the opportunity to correct that error.
This motion extends the period that a person ordered removed after inquiry has to instruct counsel from 24 hours to two weeks. There is a technical problem with the amendment because it does not provide an equivalent stay of the removal order beyond 24 hours. In any event, two weeks is unreasonably and unrealistically long. All the person concerned needs to do in 24 hours is to decide whether he wishes to seek judicial review or not and sign an affidavit authorizing counsel to act on behalf of the person concerned.
Therefore we oppose the motion.

He said: Madam Speaker, I want to thank Hon. Members for this opportunity to take part in the debate on my amendment No. 4.
Madam Speaker, I am in duty bound and even compelled by my conscience to rise in debates concerning certain amendments.
First, having been elected in 1984 and being a Member of the Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration, since the beginning, I have attended many meetings, where a number of persons have appeared, stating that what we need in Canada is a system with a refugee status that is more precise, more clear cut, easier, more understandable than the one we now have, that is before Bill C-55 was put forward.
Many people are wondering and asking me: How is it that Fernand Jourdenais, Chairman of the Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration, is the only one in his group willing to defend Bill C-55? The reason why I insist indeed on introducing certain amendments is that when the Bill was introduced in May, Members of the Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration had very strong reactions, and some even said: We worked for two and a half years and nothing, almost nothing of what we decided in report No. 5 is written down in the Bill.
There is something in the Bill, there is certainly the basic principle of having a clearer, more open and speedier system. But out of 62 pages of proposals, we have quite a problem understanding actually, when one is outside the law profession, is not a lawyer or a judge, and you know as well as I do, Madam Speaker, that one must be cautious with the so-called "small print"!
If we look at page 11 of the Bill, Clause 45, we find something which is contrary to the principle and the aim of Bill C-55.

September 18, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
We are saying it will be fair, but we can already see from this clause that it will not be fair. It will not be fair because when we have refugees entering Canada, when they first meet an immigration official or somebody who represents the law these people get nervous, they are tired, they are afraid precisely because they have just fled a country where they had problems, where authority was represented by an individual who would not think twice before throwing them behind bars and torturing them if they dared utter a single word in his presence.
According to this clause, if during the interview the adjudicator asks the refugee or the person applying for refugee status: "are you applying for refugee status?", and if that person happens to be nervous or fails to understand because there is an interpreter, and for all sorts of reasons, because he feels cornered by the authorities and because in his country he has experienced difficulties with officials and was scared, if he does not answer right away even before they begin to question him, the kind of questions which, according to the legislation, are very important, like whether or not he should be transferred to the next stage so his case can be reviewed, if he does not ask for it he will not have the right during the interview to say: I want refugee status.
This is a lengthy clause, and any ordinary man who takes a close look at it will find it hard to understand that if he fails to ask for refugee status right from the start he will be turned down later on. A man can indeed be a genuine refugee, and those who will have applied will be genuine refugees, but they will be afraid to say they want refugee status because in their country anyone making such a request is likely to be mistreated.
Witnesses gave evidence before the legislative committee; unfortunately I was not qualified to sit on that committee, but some people said, and I quote:
"The principle of immediate claim may not be compatible with the claimant's emotional state upon arrival."

Others said:

"Newly arrived refugees may be afraid to make a claim". [Translation]
This is exactly what I said earlier. Those people are so nervous-I could tell you how we had a witness one evening in committee, someone who came from Guyana; it took an hour and a half before he could speak by himself and give us answers, although ours was not the type of questioning that could have sent him to prison. All we wanted to know was what had happened when he landed in Canada, in Toronto. Finally, after an hour and a half, at 11 p.m., he started telling us what had happened during the first interview he had when
he came to Canada, with the first person he met. And he was not a fellow from the woods back in his country, he was the principal of two CEGEPS, a well-educated man, well-mannered, very knowledgeable; but he was nervous indeed because he had a wife and a four-year-old child and he was afraid he would be sent to prison, as had been done in his own country.
And if Bill C-55 was written in such a way as to be fair, the Government should accept the fact that the -majority of Canadians want a refugee determination formula that will allow indentification of genuine refugees as against the others, in order to offer them long-lasting protection in Canada. The Government should recognize that the refugee determination process should both protect genuine refugees and deter those who abuse it. Those two goals should not be considered as necessarily opposite, and the implementation of the four following criteria, which 1 hope I have time to indicate, will help us reach that goal.
First, the formula must guarantee as much as possible that legitimate refugees can be identified and protected, which Section 45 does not do. Second, the formula must be effective, which means that it must be accompanied by a fast determination process which is both economical and practical, as this is the very basis of the Bill. Third, the formula must comply with the constitutional guarantees for equity and meet the basic requirements of legal administrative tribunals. Fourth, the formula must be in tune with the international legal commitments of Canada as signatory to the United Nations Convention on Refugees, and by not allowing the claimant from saying at any time during the hearing that he claims refugee status, we are going against this Convention.
Naturally, there will be a lot of debate on this point. There has already been a lot of discussion and there will be more. However, I believe that the Government should amend Section 45 along the lines that 1 mention in Motion No. 4:

Therefore, Madam Speaker, when you realize all the good these people do in Canada after they settle down, I think it is necessary that this Section 45 be amended using the words I have just mentioned.

Madam Speaker, I am very happy to support the amendment of the Hon. Member for Fa Prairie (Mr. Jourdenais).
September 18, 1987



I commend him for the courage and generosity he has shown while defending the cause of refugees during the couple of years he was in our Committee.

1 want to emphasize a point which has been made, that it is not reasonable to expect that a genuine refugee will always make his claim at the first moment. We have plenty of experience of bogus refugees making their claims at the first moment. That is the point; they have been coached.
I am told that there were 3,600 people who came from one country in Europe saying, "I am a Jehovah's Witness; if I go back there, I will be persecuted by the Roman Catholic Church". They would have no trouble with this clause. They would shoot right ahead and make their claim at the right time, because they paid somebody several thousands of dollars to coach them on how to do it.
Those are not the people I am concerned for. Those are not the people who will be caught by this clause if we do not amend it. They will not be caught by the clause if we amend it, but there will be people who will be unfairly caught by this clause if we do not amend it. Those will be the people, as the Hon. Member for La Prairie said, who come here nervous because of what they have gone through. In all or most cases they are in fact refugees, and what they have gone through to make them refugees in many cases also makes them nervous.
To tell them in effect, to borrow the words from another context, "speak now or forever hold your peace" is unreasonable. To marry people in our church, banns are called. We are notified that so and so will be married on such a day. When the day comes, everybody in the community has had that notice. When the officiant at the marriage is about to proceed with the act of making two people husband and wife, he says: "This is the end of the time for any objection or intervention. If anybody knows why they should not be husband and wife, speak now or forever hold your peace; don't interfere later if you don't interfere now".
Somehow or other that notion, which is quite reasonable in our marriage service, has been brought in here and turned upside down. This is not the end of a long inquiry and study. This is only the beginning of it, and it is the beginning of it only if the person knows what to say at that time. For some people there may even be a language problem. Not many refugee claimants come here speaking English as their first language. Of those few who do, many of them we suspect of not being genuine refugees.
These are the people who may have a language difficulty. These are the people who may have what we could call, in a very mild sense with great understatement, a culture gap.
Recently I met a group of refugees from a Latin American district. They were refugees from a country in which, in very recent months, the military has shot people demonstrating in the streets. Unarmed people, labour groups, or other groups
Immigration Act, 1976
demonstrating in the streets for what we would consider to be normal human rights have been shot, very often beaten, and often arrested, for doing what we take for granted as normal action by citizens who wish to get together to make their point publicly.
They sought the help of my friend who made some of the arrangements which in our culture are the appropriate things to do, and who spoke their language-Spanish. When these people, newly in the country, refugees, for the purpose of this demonstration, asked my friend, "Will the police shoot at us?", she was more than a little startled by the question. When she assured them that they would not, they said: "Well, will they beat us or will they arrest us?" My friend assured them that they would not, and they asked: "How do you know they won't?" My friend brought out the police permit.
They had asked for help from people who know the ways in our country. One way is that if you are going to use the public streets for demonstration, you talk it over with the police to make sure that it will not cause undue disruption of traffic or perhaps a collision with another demonstration. That sometimes happens in Toronto streets. My friend had a police permit and showed it to these people. They were satisfied, and they came out for the demonstration.
I think those people at that point learned something about Canada, but I am glad they learned, and I believe every Member of this House is glad they learned, that in Canada demonstrators are not normally shot at, beaten or arrested by police. There may be incidents involving such things, especially arrest from time to time, but it is not the normal way that demonstrators, the police and the public conduct affairs in Canada. That illustrates the baggage that a refugee may carry with him when he comes to Canada. If I stick my neck out against authority, if I question or challenge authority, can I be shot, beaten or jailed?
I grew up in Canada. The only year I was out of town was when I was in Chicago. Sometimes Chicago has a reputation for violence, but I did not notice it because I was at the university. I have been fortunate to live in a very peaceful country. I was shocked, as my young friend was, to hear stories like that of the expectations or fears of people when they come here.
We are told by the Hon. Member for Calgary West (Mr. Hawkes) that a humanitarian element is in the Bill through a recent amendment, which was proposed in the last few hours of the committee hearings, that is supposed to help the process. I am sure the Hon. Member thinks that that will be understood in the way he intends it by all concerned. What it amounts to is another prescreening. It seems that the Government, as far as possible, is adamantly opposed to letting people state their refugee claims. The Government has now introduced prescreening. It is on page 16-at least that is what I

September 18, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
assume the Hon. Member for Calgary West refers to. Subclause (7) on page 16 reads:
If the Minister is of the opinion that the claimant has a credible basis for the claim and informs the adjudicator and the Member of the Refugee Division of that opinion, the adjudicator and the member shall determine that the claimant has a credible basis for the claim.
This is another prescreening. We will have an occasion to speak about that later, Madam Speaker, but 1 want to point out now that the Government is protecting itself massively against a person who may be a genuine refugee who wants to state his case in the place where the decision will be made. He has to pass through a series of areas. The inquiry is the main barrier, but now we are told there will be another screening before the inquiry. The Government has all these chances to stop a refugee, but it gives him only one chance to say the word that could be a matter of life and death, freedom or imprisonment if he is a genuine refugee.
We have heard a lot of nonsense about how many people are not genuine refugees. I call it nonsense because the figures have been inflated and distorted, sometimes by those who know better. Our committee found two years ago that a majority of the people who had been examined turned out to be either bona fide refugees or worthy of having the humanitarian programs of our Government and country applied on their behalf. That was a system unfair to the refugee claimant, according to the decision of our Supreme Court, because most of the claimants had not had an oral hearing before those who would make the decision about them. Even by an unfair test, over half of the claimants had been found to be either bona fide refugees or to be worthy of humanitarian protection even though they were not exactly refugees. We should not be so hasty to cut them off. We should not be so hasty to cut them off at the very first chance they have to make their case.

Madam Speaker, it is quite a trick to deal with nine amendments in 10 minutes, which is the consequence of the grouping. I would like to commend the Hon. Member for La Prairie (Mr. Jourdenais) for his diligence on the committee over many months. I think the committee report was presented in November, 1985. Perhaps it is time that he reread it. I think some of the things he said earlier this day about that report are not accurate. Bill C-55 is absolutely remarkable in the degree to which it is a faithful reproduction of committee recommendations.
Regarding the whole issue of review, the committee recommended a two-person oral hearing with the benefit of the claim going to the claimant with leave to appeal to the Federal Court of Canada. That is exactly what Bill C-55 does. The basic principle of benefit to the claimant runs throughout the Bill. Provision of counsel which the committee recommended runs throughout the Bill. The presence of a refugee board member at every stage of the proceedings, not just the refugee claim, but the issue of removal and departure, is guaranteed by the Bill. The notion of a safe Third Country was deliberately included, not with that language, in our committee report and approved by all three Parties.
It is a little disturbing to listen to statements in this House and statements made in the press about how discrepant this Bill is from what the committee recommended. It is not, and the Bill goes beyond what the committee recommended in its fairness to legitimate refugees. It goes beyond any sense of speed for removal of abusers. There is absolutely no disagreement in Canada that maximum speed for the removal of abusers is not only justified but desirable. I commend the drafters for finding something faster, a series of ways dealing with the situation, than committee members could find. The Bill is very faithful to the principles of the committee report.
I have tried to look at these nine amendments and ask myself, how do we deal with them in what probably now is seven minutes instead of 10? There are absurdities. The motion from the Hon. Member for La Prairie and the motion from the Liberal Party of Canada create the following absurdities which exist in the current law. There is no end for the abuser. There has to be a point at which a claim is made and when that point is passed the person has the opportunity to claim to be a refugee so one can get on to other things. When opposition Members ask us to accept an amendment in this Chamber that provides no such point, an absurdity is created. It becomes impossible to remove someone from this country.
There are about 1,000 people a month who are discovered by immigration enforcement officers to have broken the Immigration Act, to be living and working here illegally, or whatever. The current system has no such point. Three-quarters of these people, 750 a month, are already inside this country legally or illegally, and the minute they face the inquiry for removal they claim to be refugees and five years later maybe we can kick them out. That has to stop, Madam Speaker. When an inquiry for removal begins, every single human being appearing before that inquiry has the right to a taxpayer-paid barrister and solicitor. They have counsel. The question is very simple. Are you a refugee? Yes or no. Counsel can act for the claimant and say yes. That is how simple it is.
We hear of all sorts of examples of frightened human beings. That becomes apparent during an inquiry. The inquiries are not simply an hour and a half long. Seldom will an inquiry on the issue of a removal be anything short of three days. Very commonly they will last at least a week and in some cases three or four weeks.
Bill C-84 allows for detention for 28 days without review by adjudicators for undocumented arrivals. Some 10,000 of them had to be referred to the RCMP for help this year. After all, an inquiry cannot be started until the identity of the person involved is known.
These fears are false. It is true that frightened people arrive in Canada. It is true that frightened people may arrive in Canada from Guyana. This law requires the past history of nationals of a particular country and its refugee claimants to be taken into consideration by the adjudicator and the refugee
September 18, 1987

board member. Guyana is a country that produces refugees. That is an evidentiary fact which must be entered on the record and must be taken into account by the adjudicator and the refugee board member. When it is evident that people are coming from a refugee-producing country, their cases must go before the board. That is what the Bill provides.
It is time we stopped dealing with the mythology surrounding this Bill and started dealing with its reality. As a group, these amendments eliminate the possibility for fast determination of bogus claimants. There is not a church group, human rights activist or any Canadian with any credibility who appeared before the committee who did not urge fast removal of bogus claimants. We will eat up all of our resources and all of the good will that exists in Canada toward bogus claimants if we cannot remove them quickly. Removing them quickly is the only way to stop others from arriving.
Some of these amendments try to get rid of the notion of eligibility. Eligibility is determined by an adjudicator and a refugee board member. What are the criteria of eligibility?
First is the question of whether or not the refugee needs the protection of Canada. Those who are already Convention refugees or who have come from a safe third country are not eligible. No one can guarantee absolute safety for every individual in every country we will put on that list, but there will not be many countries that will be unsafe. I suggest that most of the countries on the list will be European, and I suggest that people are as safe there as they would be here.
We do not want to see the constant movement of claimants from country to country. Some claimants have claims existing in three or four western countries all at the same time. The resources of three or four countries are going to a single individual. Are these people, the ones who are already in western European countries like Sweden, Denmark, Holland, France and Britain the most likely to be in need of Canada's protection? No, they are a low priority. The person from Guyana, from El Salvador, from the Middle East or from Asia is the person who needs our help. Therefore, the first eligibility criterion is whether or not the claimants need our help. If they are from a country on the list or if their cases have been determined, they do not need our help.
The next criterion relates to repeat claims or to going past the time when a claim ought to be made. That is a Canadian determination. Those who have already been found not to be refugees or chose not to claim are not eligible. Can we have an endless chain as proposed by these amendments? Should we let a claimant make another claim every time we try to remove him? There would be 10 hearings, 20 hearings, 40 hearings, an infinite number of hearings. That is absolutely absurd and is unfair to legitimate claimants. There must be a moment when the claim is made, the determination is made and removal follows. Failure to remove would be an absolute catastrophe for the system.
What is the third criterion? The Standing Committee report of a year ago June said that it had grave doubts about the
Immigration Act, 1976
protection offered to Canada by the Immigration Act and its processes. Therefore, the third eligibility criterion is security. In a case where there are security questions, instead of going to the board, it would go directly to a federal court judge who would determine whether or not the person is a danger to Canada.
We cannot be the patsies of the world. It is time we toughened the immigration laws and took away the loophole that creates a wide-open door to potential terrorism in Canada. I commend the Government for moving on this matter.
There is not one amendment in this grouping of nine that does not do serious damage to our ability to remove abusers. There is nothing in these provisions that does serious damage in any way, shape or form to legitimate refugee claimants. I believe that the parts of the Bill covered by these amendments should stay as they are.

Madam Speaker, it is very difficult to maintain one's composure when one hears the kind of comments made by the Hon. Member. Either he does not understand what has been said by all of the groups representing refugees and by all of the distinguished lawyers who appeared before the committee or he is purposely twisting the views of those groups.
He said that all of these groups are in favour of fast removal of abusers. Sure, they are in favour of that, but they are not in favour of a prescreening process which will not allow claimants full hearings on the merits, and he knows that. He knows about the flaws of this Bill. Nonetheless, he is trying to wrap himself in the flag.
Earlier today, the Hon. Member said that this is the most humanitarian and the best kind of refugee determination process in the world and that it will tell us who all the refugees are. I would like to refer the Hon. Member to the comments of Mr. Arthur Helton of the Lawyers' Committee for Human Rights. Mr. Helton is no slouch. He is an adjunct professor teaching immigration and asylum law at New York University School of Law, the North American co-ordinator of an exchange of legal practitioners under the auspices of the European Consultation on Refugees and Exiles, a practitioner in the United States and a student of other systems. He said that in other countries in Europe where the concept of a safe Third Country has been introduced, the determination is made on an individual basis. It is part and parcel of the process of determining whether a person is in need of protection. It is not an arbitrary decision made on the basis of whether or not a person comes from a country which is on a list prepared by Cabinet, a list subject to all the political considerations about which the standing committee has been warned.
Mr. Helton, when appearing before the committee, said the following:
Virtually all the countries that utilize the first asylum principle regard it on
an individual basis, and in making a determination decide whether or not to
assess the intent or wishes of the individual. I would particularly cite Austria,
France, Sweden, and the United Kingdom.

September 18, 1987
Yellowknife Electric Ltd.
The Elon. Member has said that this law is equivalent to practice which is acceptable in other countries. Ele has said that it will provide safeguards and that individual refugees will always be given the benefit of the doubt, the favourite expression of the Minister of State for Immigration (Mr. Weiner). What he has said is totally at variance with the facts and totally at variance with everything that was said before the legislative committee which studied this Bill. It is totally at variance with ail knowledgeable opinions expressed by editorial and opinion comments in the newspapers over the course of the past several months.
There are many more things I could say about the extraordinary contentions being made by members of the Government, but I see it is past two o'clock and we will get another crack at this next week.

PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-PRIVATE BILLS   YELLOWKNIFE ELECTRIC LTD.
speechtext:
that Bill S-10, an Act to revive Yellowknife Electric Ltd. and to provide for its continuance under the Canada Business Corporations Act, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.
He said: Madam Speaker, I am happy to speak to this particular Bill which, in summary, is the situation of a corporation in all innocence ceasing to exist under the laws of Canada and seeking to have new life breathed into it so it can effectively wind down its affairs and continue on. The Bill was sponsored in the other place by the Hon. Senator Nathan Nurgitz. It is an Act to revive Yellowknife Electric Ltd. and provide for its continuance under the Canada Business Corporations Act. The Bill was passed by the Senate on June 16th of this year, by unanimous consent, and I hope we might have unanimous consent to pass it through all stages today, depending upon the disposition of other Parties.
Yellowknife Electric Ltd. was incorporated on March 21, 1955, by letters patent issued under the Companies Act. The company's principal place of business is in the City of Yellowknife in the Northwest Territories. Subsection 125(1) of the Companies Act requires that the company file with the Department of the Secretary of State an annual summary. Yellowknife Electric Ltd. failed to file those summaries for three consecutive years. As is required under the law, notice of the company's failure to file the prescribed annual summary was published in The Canada Gazette on June 11 and June 20, 1966, stating that Yellowknife Electric Ltd. would be dissolved unless within one year of the publication the company filed the summaries for the three years in respect of which it was in default. Those prescribed summaries were not filed. As a consequence, Yellowknife Electric Ltd. was dissolved pursuant to Subsection 125(12) of the Canada Corporations Act.
When we examine the facts of the case, the directors of the company did not see, nor did they have any knowledge of, the default in filing annual summaries. It may be the duty of all of us to read prodigiously and religiously all the contents of The Canada Gazette, but some of us are remiss in that regard. Apparently the notices to file were sent to the registered office
September 18, 1987

of the company, a lawyer's office, and the solicitors for the company omitted to file same. The directors of the company simply did not know why the annual summaries were not filed. The solicitors for the company did not have any record of the notices, nor do they recollect the circumstances of the default in filing the summaries.
1 and my staff have gone to some pains to determine these facts are accurate because even though this may seem like a small matter, we are proposing to occupy some time of Hon. Members and of this House in making a determination of this particular Bill. So I can speak with some conviction when I say that these facts are accurate as stated.
The company, unaware of the order published in The Canada Gazette on June 24, 1967, dissolving Yellowknife Electric Ltd., continued to carry on business as if it had not been dissolved. It will not be possible for the company to continue to carry on business unless it is revived. Assets are trapped inside the company and cannot be dealt with by the company as Yellowknife Electric Ltd. is technically not a legal entity. For example, the directors have no capacity to transfer land owned by the company, nor would the Land Titles Office register a transfer without a certificate of good standing of the corporation. The certificate is of course impossible to obtain because without revival there is no company. The company has complied with required publication requirements. The company has no liabilities whatsoever.
To address the question of why the Bill is in the House today, the Companies Act as amended, Revised Statutes of Canada 1952, Chapter 53, had no revival provisions for a company dissolved in circumstances such as applied in the case of Yellowknife Electric Ltd. This, with respect, could be described as a legislative oversight. Rare as those may be, this appears to be one. However, today's legislation allows revival of the dissolved corporation as an administrative matter. One simply files articles of revival with the director of corporations and the director shall issue a certificate of revival. That appears under the terms of the Canada Business Corporations Act, Statutes of Canada, 1984, 1985, 1986, Chapter 33.
Since the company was a corporation to which Part I of the Canada Corporations Act applied, and since there is no provision in this Act for revival of a company that has been dissolved, the company cannot be revived except by a special Act of the Parliament of Canada.
With respect to the matter of continuance, if the company had not been dissolved it would have been required to apply on or before December 15, 1980, for a certificate of continuance pursuant to the Canada Business Corporations Act.
Let me give some background on the company. The company has its objects set out in the letters patent. They provide that the Yellowknife Electric Ltd. is in the business of electrical and plumbing contracting. At this moment, it is winding down its affairs in Yellowknife. I am informed that it
Yellowknife Electric Ltd.
is the intention of the company to relocate and carry on business in Vancouver, British Columbia. It owns substantial assets, including a block of realty in Yellowknife in the Northwest Territories.
The company has no liabilities. It made an attempt to sell the realty and, in fact, accepted an interim agreement for sale and purchase, when they were made aware that the company had been struck in 1967.
The registrar of land titles in the Northwest Territories would not accept the transfer without a certificate of good standing of the corporation and this was, of course, impossible to provide as the company was dissolved.
I believe it was at this stage that it was discovered that this Bill would be necessary and that it would be necessary for the Parliament of Canada to become active in the case.
As I said at the outset, I hope the House might be disposed to deal with this matter today. I hoped that would be the case, but I am given to understand that it may not be.
In any event, I hope the facts as I have been able to outline them will be of some benefit to Hon. Members in determining the fate of this company. There was innocence, perhaps some neglect, if not negligence on the part of certain individuals in positions of trust. 1 am given to understand that at least one of them may have been rather elderly at the time that the responsibility was on his shoulders. I hope Members might consider the circumstances and give some consideration to the affairs of the company so that it could be restored to person-hood, one might say, and continue the objects of the directors of the company.
